G.S.R. 188.—In exercise of the powers conferred by section 139 of the National Security Guard Act, 1986 
(47 of 1986), the Central Government hereby makes the following rules to amend the National Security Guard (Group 
‘C’ posts) Recruitment Rules, 2004, namely: - 


(1) These rules may be called the National Security Guard (Group ‘C’ posts) Recruitment (Amendment) 
Rules, 2025. 


(2)They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. In the National Security Guard (Group ‘C’ posts) Recruitment Rules, 2004, in the Schedule, against serial 
number 9 relating to the post of Ranger-I/Ranger-II Combatised Tradesman (General Duty/Technical & 
Tradesman/Administrative), in column (12), under the heading Deputation, in clause (ii), for the figures and word 
“45 years’, the figures and word “50 years” shall be substituted. 


[F. No. 1-13011/1/RR/2025/ HQ NSG/5042] 
P.S. DANGWAL, Director 


Note : The principal rules were published in the Gazette of India, Part-II, Section 3, Sub-section (i), vide number 
G.S.R. 422, dated the 10" December, 2004.

G.S.R. 189.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution and in 


supersession of the National Savings Institute (Group C posts) Recruitment Rules, 2012, except as respects things 
done or omitted to be done before such supersession, the President hereby makes the following rules regulating the 
method of recruitment of the post of Upper Division Clerk, Lower Division Clerk and Multi-Tasking Staff in the 
National Savings Institute, Delhi under the Ministry of Finance, namely :- 


1. 


Short title and commencement.- (1) These rules may be called the National Savings Institute (Group ‘C’ 
posts) Recruitment Rules, 2025. 
(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 
Number of posts, classification and level in the pay matrix. - The number of the said posts, its 
classification and the level in the pay matrix attached thereto shall be as specified in columns (2) to (4) of the 
Schedule annexed to these rules. 
Method of recruitment, age limit and other qualifications etc.- The method of recruitment, age- limit, 
qualifications and other matters relating to the said post shall be as specified in columns (5) to (14) of the 
said Schedule. 
Initial Constitution.- The incumbents of the post shown in column(1) of the Schedule annexed to these rules 
who were appointed on regular basis to the post in the National Savings Institute which has been restructured 
vide Resolution dated the 77 March, 2022 of Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance before 
the commencement of these rules, shall be deemed to have been appointed under these rules and the service 
rendered by them in the said post before the commencement of these rules shall be taken into account for the 
purpose of level in the pay matrix, Promotion and Pension, etc. 
Disqualification. - No person,- 

(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having a spouse living; or 

(b) who having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person; 
shall be eligible for appointment to the said post : 


Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal law 
applicable to such person and the other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for doing so, exempt 
any person from the operation of this rule. 


6. Power to relax. — Where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient to do so, 
it may by order, for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax any of the provisions of these rules in respect of 
any class or category of persons. 

7. Saving. - Nothing in these rules shall affect reservations, relaxation of age-limit and other concessions 
required to be provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Ex- 
servicemen and other special categories of persons, in accordance with the orders issued by the Central

2. All the aforementioned cases were received from the Ministry of Labour on 21.06.2002. After receipt of 
reference, both parties were noticed, the workmen filed their written statements on 22.08.2002 and the management 
also filed their written statement-cum-rejoinder on 28.11.2002. 


3. All the above reference cases have been heard analogously as all the four cases are identical in nature. 


4. It is relevant to mention that previously these cases were decided by this Tribunal by passing award dated 
03.12.2013 but when the same were challenged by the management before the Hon’ble High Court of Jharkhand, 
Ranchi, the award passed by this Tribunal was set aside and the case was remanded for passing fresh award on the 
basis of the evidence already available on the case record. 


5. The case of the workmen in short is that the workmen concerned were working at D.V.C., Foreshore Farm, 
Sewai since long to the satisfaction of all concerned and they worked continuously till 25.04.2000 but their services 
were terminated by the order of Sri J. Singh, Dy. Director of Soil Conservation (R & T), Soil Conservation 
Department, D.V.C., Hazaribagh. The management of D.V.C. took their services to deprive them from legitimate 
claims showing them as the contractor’s workers by camouflaging the real issue through paper arrangements. When 
the workmen demanded regularization of their services in D.V.C., the Dy. Director, Soil Conservation became furious 
and issued a letter to Farm In charge Foreshore Farm, Sewai and directed to stop the services of the concerned 
workmen and further directed to recruit other workmen in their places. The Dy. Director has not shown any reason for 
the termination of the services of the workmen. Their termination is a glaring example of hire and fire. D.V.C. is a 
public sector undertaking and such type of unfair labour practice not expected from such organization. The decision 
of the Dy. Director is illegal and unjustified. The workmen have never committed any misconduct during their service 
period and therefore they are entitled for reinstatement with full back wages and at last it was prayed to hold that the 
action of the management in terminating the services of the workmen concerned is neither legal nor justified and 
direct the management to reinstate them with full back wages and other benefits. 


6. On the other hand the case of the management in short is that the reference is bad in as much as Fulchand 
Saw (Ref. No. 61/2002), Baijnath Mistry (Ref. No. 62/2002), Chhotan Mahato (Ref. No. 63/2002) and Kartik Mahto 
(Ref. No. 64/2002) were never workmen and as such there was no question of termination of their services. The 
statement made in Para 3 of the written statement of the workmen are not correct. Since the workmen were working 
on job contract basis and they are working under a leader of job contractor, there could not be any question of 
terminating their services by J. Singh, Deputy Director of Soil Conservation. The statement made in Para 4 are also 
not true and correct. Since workmen were casual labour, there was no question of taking work from them. The 
concerned workmen were paid on the basis of quantum of work and not on the basis of their daily presence. The 
quantum of work done by them was entered in the measurement book and paid accordingly through their leader. It is 
denied that the persons concerned were workmen in D.V.C. All the works of job contract are based on the specified 
rate of its particular item based on minimum wages. The statement made in Para 5 are also not true. The persons 
concerned along with others filed a writ application before the Ranchi Bench of Hon’ble Patna High Court in CWJC 
No. 2303/94 (R) which was decided by the Hon’ble Court on 24.11.1995 wherein and whereby it was categorically 
found that the persons concerned were engaged on job contract basis and therefore payments were made on the basis 
of the measurement book as per piece rated meant for the job and there was no question for regularizing of their 
services. The statement made in Para 6, 7 and 8 are also not true and correct. In the account of statement before the 
Hon’ble High Court the position was made clear that the petitioners were employed as job contractor leader and not 
as workman or casual workman and therefore their claim cannot be considered. It is denied that there is any 
victimization or that the persons concerned are entitled to reinstatement with full back wages. The statements made in 
Para 9 to 11 of the W/S of the workmen are not correct. There is no question of unfair labour practice or that the 
persons concerned were terminated by the Deputy Director. Since the persons concerned were not workmen, the 
question of reinstatement on full back wages does not arise. The statement made in Para 13 and 14 of the W/S are also 
not true and correct as they are not the workmen, so there is no question of following the procedure. As a matter of 
fact on the basis of the Hon’ble High Court order, representation was made before the Director Human Resources 
Development DVC, Calcutta which was turned down in view of the aforesaid facts that they were on job under a 
contract and not a workman and at last it was prayed to decide the reference against the persons concerned as they do 
not come under the purview of the Industrial Dispute Act.

The Ld. Counsel for the workmen has submitted that the workmen concerned were working at DVC Foreshore

Court in Waterfront Workers Case of 2001 and so this Tribunal has no jurisdiction to pass award in this case and 
prayed to reject the Reference.

has not even whispered on this point in its WS and only at the time of argument, he has orally challenged the 
jurisdiction of this Tribunal in deciding these Ref. cases which have been duly referred to this Tribunal by the Central 
Government and secondly, whatever was held in relation to the appropriate government in case of Steel Authority of 
India Ltd. & Ors vs National Union Water Front Workers & Ors of the year 2001, by the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court, that was only for the purpose of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act but that is not the issue here

15. As regards the oral testimony of the management, MW-1 Dr. S. Sengupta has deposed in all the 4 Ref. cases 
that he was looking after the affairs of Research and Training under the Research and Training (R & T) Division at 
DVC. He has deposed that the Soil Conservation Department of the management corporation carries on the work of 
soil conservation which besides other things, includes the work of aforestation, plantation, farming etc. in and around 
the area of Damodar Valley. All these works are purely seasonal in nature which is carried on with the help of local 
people of the particular area concerned. The management had been doing the work of foreshore farming at Sewai, 
Bundu, Urwan etc. for the benefit of the farmers of the locality. As per the prevailing practice, tilling of soil, 
plantation of seedlings and other incidental works were being assigned to a particular person of the area on job 
contract basis who in turn engaged required number of hands for doing a particular work. Such job contract used to be 
assigned to different persons for different works and different areas and payment used to be made to that particular 
person through Hand Receipts on the basis of measurement of the job recorded in the Measurement Book at the rate 
fixed by the management corporation from time to time on the basis of minimum wages fixed by the State 
Government. The person who might have worked under the said job contract are not the workmen within the meaning 
of the I.D. Act nor has there been any employer-employee relationship between the management corporation and the 
concerned workmen. The allegation of the workmen that they had been working in the foreshore farm at Sewai since 
long and that the management has terminated their services on 25.04.2000 is misconceived. It is also wrong to say 
that the workmen had rendered the alleged services as Contract Labour or otherwise. The Concerned workmen had 
filed writ petition before the Hon’ble Patna High Court claiming their regularization but their writ petition was 
disposed of by the Hon’ble Court vide order dated 24.01.1995 holding that there was no dispute between the parties 
with regard to the nature of job performed by them and accordingly directed to file petition before the DVC and 
accordingly they filed the representations but the concerned authorities of the corporation passed an order that there 
being no provision for such regularization, there was no scope for the same nor could the corporation frame a policy 
in this connection and they were not their employees. Thereafter the workmen did not assail the said order of the 
management and after long lapse of times they have raised industrial dispute, five others raised similar disputes before 
the State Govt. which was referred to the Ld. Labour Court, Hazaribagh and therefore the present reference is not 
legally maintainable under the facts and circumstances and the demand of the concerned workmen for reinstatement 
with back wages is also not maintainable and they are not entitled to any relief. In the cross-examination he has 
admitted that the certificates have been issued by the Office which belongs to their office. D.V.C is in Jharkhand and 
West Bengal. It is a corporation of Central Govt. They have taken work of the concerned workmen through gang 
leader. Payment is made to the contractor on job contract basis. They have got no agreement for job contractor with 
gang leader and they have not filed any license of the contractor. Payment is made to the workers as per Minimum 
Wages Act. They have not filed any paper specifying particular work in particular time. Workers payment sheet has 
not been filed. They do not take attendance of the workers, they take work through gang leader of the whole year. It is 
not a fact that they have retrenched the concerned workmen as they have not appointed them.

Baijnath Mistry in Ref no. 62/2000, Chhotan Mahto in Ref. Case no. 63/2000 and Kartik Mahto in ref case 
no.64/2000. The documentary evidence of the management also reveals that the workmen were working on job 
contract basis (Exhibit M-1) and MW1 has admitted in his cross-examination that the documents of the workmen 
were issued from his office. In the documents of workmen (Ext.W 1 Series) also the status of the workmen have been 
shown mentioning that they were working on job contract basis. 


18. The management has contended that the workmen who have been working as job contract labour cannot be 
treated to be the workmen u/s 2(s) of the ILD. Act, 1947 and therefore they can not claim any relief of 
reinstatement/regularization in this case in view of Uma Devi Case. In this regard the Hon’ble Supreme Court has 
held in case of Dharangdhara Chemical Works Ltd. Vs. State of Saurashtra reported in AIR 1957 SC 264 that 
there is abundant authority in England that a person can be a workman even though he is paid not per day but by the 
job. Similar view was taken in Maharaja Bidi Factory case reported in 1958(2) LLJ 736 But the test is whether the 
employer retains the power of controlling the work and it makes no difference whether the man was employed on a 
daily wage or was paid by the job. 


19. Here in the instant case also on perusal of Exhibit W-1 series it transpires that all the certificates have been 
issued under the signature and stamp of Farm Incharge Foreshore Farm, SCD, DVC, Sewai (also admitted by MW1 in 
cross-examination) and similarly the copy of letter dated 24.05.2000 written by J. Singh to Farm Incharge, Fore Shore 
directing him to stop the workmen from job contract duty with immediate effect (Ref Case no. 62/2000) goes to 
establish the direct control of the management on work of the workmen concerned and it is sufficient to infer that 
there is a relationship of employer and employee between the management and the workmen. The Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has very recently held in case of Jaggo vs Union of India reported in 2024 INSC 1034 that the principles of 
Uma Devi Case should not be misinterpreted to deny the legitimate claims and it does not intend to penalize 
employees who have rendered long years of services in ongoing and necessary functions of the state. 


20. Thus, on the basis of above appreciations of facts, circumstances and evidences available on the case record 
the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the action of the management of DVC in terminating the services of 
Fulchand Saw(Ref. No. 61/2002), BaijnathMistry(Ref. No. 62/2002), ChhotanMahto(Ref. No. 63/2002) and 
KartikMahto (Ref. No. 64/2002) is not justified and the management is directed to reinstate the services of the 
workmen with all consequential benefits from the date of their termination. So this issue is also decided in favour of 
the workmen and this reference is answered accordingly.

New Delhi for information and notification.

2. It is relevant to mention here that the present reference case no. 323 of 2000 was previously decided by this 


Tribunal by passing Award dated 24.12.2014 but when the management challenged the same by filing W.P.(L) 
No. 2144 of 2015, the Hon’ble High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi vide order dated 03.07.2024 was pleased to set 
aside the Award passed by this Tribunal holding the same as cryptic and remitted back the case record to this Tribunal 
with direction for passing a fresh Award on the basis of the materials which are already available on the record. 


3. The case of the workmen as per the written statement filed on 12.09.2001 is that the Rajmahal Project, 
Lalmatia, Godda, one of the coal producing unit of M/s. Eastern Coalfields Ltd. is a Government undertaking 
company of Govt. of India. There is a Pirpainty Railway Siding/Pirpainty Coal Dump at Bhagalpur, Bihar. The coal 
produced at Rajmahal Project, Lalmatia are transported by road to the Pirpainty Railway Siding (known as Pirpainty 
coal dump and dumped there). The dumped coal at Pirpainty Railway Siding are transported by road from Rajmahal 


7350 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 6, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 15, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Project are dispatched through railway wagon from there to the different customers of M/s. Eastern Coalfields Ltd. 
like Kahalgaon Thermal Power Station, Farrukka Thermal Power Station, Barauni Thermal Power Station etc. During 
the course of coal transporting from Rajmahal Project to Pirpainty Railway Siding by road and coal dispatching from 
Pirpainty Railway Siding to the different customers of M/s. Eastern Coalfields Ltd. by the railway wagon the 
following works are carried out :- 


(a) Coals are loaded to the trucks from Rajmahal Projects to Pirpainty Railway Siding. 

(b) The loaded coal trucks are transported from Rajmahal Projects to Pirpainty Railway Siding. 
(c) The coal loaded trucks are unloaded at the Pirpainty Railway Siding and coal dumped there. 
(d) The dumped coals are broken as per required size and shale picking is done. 

(e) The specifically required coals are loaded to the railway wagon. 

(f) The coal loaded to the railway wagon are levelled. 


(g) And other allied jobs and dispatch. 


For carrying out the work as described above the management of Rajmahal Project M/s. Eastern Coalfields 
Ltd. deployed departmental employees as well as contractor’s employees. The management of Rajmahal Projects M/s 
Eastern Coalfields Ltd. engaged contractors for carrying out the jobs of loading and unloading etc of the coal. The 
management of Rajmahal Project M/s. ECL time to time changed the contractors for carrying out the job of loading 
and unloading of the coal etc but the workers are almost the same. The name of one of the important contractor 
engaged by the M/s. Eastern Coalfields Ltd. for carrying out the job of loading and unloading etc of the coal is M/s 
Calcutta Industrial Supply Corporation. The workers whose names have been mentioned in Annexure ‘A’ concerning 
to this dispute have been performing the jobs since 1986 continuously but they are doing the jobs of unloading the 
coal mostly at Pirpainty Railway Siding transported from Rajmahal Project by road there. During the course of 
performing the job at Pripainty Railway Siding all the equipments tools, accessories, safety equipments etc are 
provided by the contractors as well as by the management of Rajmahal Project M/s. Eastern Coalfields Ltd. Since 
1986 to 1995 the management of Rajmahal Project as well as the contractor engaged for carrying out the job of coal 
unloading from trucks, coal loading to the wagons, coal levelling, shale picking etc by deploying the concerned 
workmen and others by manually. The concerned workmen are not even being paid the minimum wages for the job 
performed by them. They also have been deprived of all legal benefits etc. as framed for the coal workers under 
several Acts like Mines Act, CMPF Act, P.G. Act, Pension etc. by the Govt. of India. The concerned workmen have 
also not been provided with the wages, Perks, Allowances, Social Securities, Welfare Amenities etc. as provided in 
the National Coal Wage Agreement for the coal workers. M/s. Eastern Coalfield Ltd. is the Principal Employer for the 
contract workers engaged by them. M/s. Eastern Coalfield Ltd as well as the contractors engaged by them for carrying 
out the job at Pirpainty Railway Siding have intentionally violated the provisions of Contract Labour Abolition and 
Regulation Act and deprived the concerned workmen of the same. The management of Rajmahal Project violated the 
provisions of Standing Order applicable to the establishment concerning to the workmen of this dispute. The 
concerned workmen demanded for their permanent absorption in M/s Eastern Coalfields Ltd. and wages, Perks, 
Allowances, Social Securities, Welfare Amenities etc as provided to the permanent workers to the establishment. The 
management of Rajmahal Project M/s. ECL in connivance with the contractors engaged by them to deny the 
legitimate demand of the concerned workmen and to make the workmen concerned jobless started introduction of 
machine by Pay Loader Dumper etc. in the year 1996. The workmen and the union of the workmen started agitation 
against the anti-labour policy and act of the management of Rajmahal Project of M/s. ECL and the contractors 
engaged by them. The workmen started Dharna etc there. After a great struggle by the workmen as well as the union 
of the workmen, the intervention of the district administration Bhagalpur and the Labour Department, the 
management of Rajmahal Project of M/s. Eastern Coalfields Ltd. and the contractors engaged by them have agreed to 
deploy the concerned workmen in the job performed by them and accordingly the workmen deployed to work as 
earlier. The workmen concerned are still in their work and the management of Rajmahal Project and the contractors 
engaged by them for the same are still violating the provision of law and victimizing the workmen concerned and 
depriving them by not providing proper wages and facilities etc. The work performed by the concerned workmen are 
of permanent and perennial in nature and are of prohibited category. There are six thousands tone of coal transported 
from Rajmahal Project to Pirpainty Railway Siding/Pirpainty Coal dump daily and the same was unloaded by the 
concerned workmen besides other works. The wages of the concerned workmen paid by the contractor are much less

13. Issue 


Whether the demand of the union from the management of Rajmahal Project of Eastern Coalfield Ltd. 
Lalmatia Godda for considering the 84 workmen (as per list) engaged under contractors for the last 13 years for

15. Now, as regards the documentary evidence adduced from the side of the workmen, on perusal of Exhibit W-

CISC Coal Dump, Pirpainty, Bhagalpur and not in the year 1986 though the words “since 1986 to 1997” have also 
been mentioned thereon. But two things are clear from this document: first, that these ID Cards have been created and 
issued by the contractor CISC and not by the ECL management and secondly, these have been created and issued by 
the signature of 15.09.97 and not in the year 1986. So it further clarifies that the concerned workmen are the 
employees of the contractor CISC and not of the ECL and it appears that these documents have been created in the 
year 1997 only to claim absorption. 


On perusal of Exhibit W-3 it transpires that this is Tripartite Agreement among ECL, Management CISC 
(BLA) and the union arrived at on 27.07.2005 and it shows that this is related to the unloading work and 84 working 
labourers and it has been agreed that all of them will be handed over the appointment letter on 28.07.2005 by the 
CISC (BLA) having full details of the salary, PF, Pension and other benefits. There are other points of agreement also 
regarding the payment of bonus in national holidays, payment of salary within time etc. On perusal of this Tripartite 
Agreement it is evident that all these 84 workmen are employed in the work of unloading of coal in Pirpainty Railway 
Siding Coal Dump by the contractor CISC and he has to give the appointment letters having full description of service 
conditions to the workmen and this is also evident that there is no demand of their absorption in this agreement. 
Likewise Exhibit W-3/1 is the Memorandum of Settlement arrived at under section 12(3) of the 1.10. Act 1947 among 
the management of CISC, M/s. Rajmahal Area of ECL and the Union Bhartiya Coal Dump Mazdoor Sangh, Pirpainty

that as many as 15 points have been settled including the payment of wages etc. It further transpires from this 
document that the management of Rajmahal Area of M/s. ECL is in practice of awarding contract since 1990 to M/s. 
CISC and M/s. BLA but at present M/s. BLA has no concern in this award but the work force are continuing since 
1990. 


Thus these both Exhibits ie Ext.W 3 & W 3/1 establish that these agreements have been entered into much 
after the reference of this case and all the concerned workmen are working under the direct control of the contractor 
CISC since 1990 and not under the direct control of the management of Rajmahal Area of M/s. ECL and no 
relationship of employer and employee is thus created between the concerned workmen and the ECL management 
because as per the terms of agreement the Contractor has to provide the workmen the appointment letters having full 
details of wages and all other benefits etc and as per para 28 of the WS of workmen admittedly their wages are paid 
by the contractor therefore, the concerned workmen can not legally claim their absorption and other benefits from the 
principal employer for the above reason as well as for want of any appointment letter, wage slip, ID Cards etc directly 
issued by the M/s ECL itself. 


16. The learned counsel for the workmen has also attracted the attention of this Tribunal towards the notification 
of the Central Government dated 217 June 1988 that has been issued in exercise of the powers conferred by Sub- 
section (1) of Section 10 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and vide this notification the 
Central Government has prohibited the employment of contract labour in the works as given in schedule of the same 
in which there is also mention of coal loading and unloading on serial no. 2 and has further submitted that the 
concerned workmen have been doing the prohibited category of work and therefore they are entitled to be absorbed in 
the permanent job of the company. He has also attracted the attention of this Tribunal towards the authority of the 
Hon’ble Supreme Court in case of Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. Vs. Brajrajnagar Coal Mines Workers Union 
reported in 2024 SCC OnLine SC 270 in which the management had regularized 19 contract workers out of 32 and 
when the dispute was raised before the Industrial Tribunal by the rest of the contract workers their case being identical 
to all those workers who were regularized, was allowed and at last the Hon’ble Apex Court also affirmed the same but 
this Tribunal is of the opinion that the facts and circumstances of this case are a bit different from the case in hand 
because there is no previous agreement between the management of ECL and the Contract workers union for 
regularization of some of the workers leaving others similarly situated. 


17. Now, as regards the point as to whether after the notification of the Central Government regarding the 
prohibition of the work of coal loading and unloading by contract labour, all the concerned 84 workmen should be 
regularized. In this regard the Hon’ble Supreme Court in case of The Directors Steel Authority Of India Ltd. Vs. 
Ispat Khadan Janta Mazdoor Union, reported in [2019] 9 S.C.R.123, has been pleased to hold that the exposition 
of the judgment of the Constitution Bench of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Steel Authority Of India Ltd and 
Others vs National Waterfront Workers and Others made it clear that neither section 10 nor any other provision in 
the CLRA Act provides for automatic absorption of contract labour on issuing a notification by the appropriate 
Government under Section 10(1) of the CLRA Act and consequently the principal employer is not required or is 
under legal obligation by operation of law to absorb the contract labour working in the establishment unless the 
contract is found to be a mere ruse to evade compliance with various beneficial legislations so as to deprive the

workers of statutory benefits. But here in the instant case, the workmen have failed to prove by any cogent evidence 
that the contract is mere sham to deprive the workmen of statutory benefits and so there is no question of the 
automatic absorption of the concerned workmen. 


18. Thus, on the basis of the above appreciation of facts, circumstances and evidence available on the case 
record, this Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the concerned workmen have failed to establish that they are legally 
entitled to permanent absorption as the employees of the ECL management and accordingly it is held that the demand 
of the union from the management of Rajmahal Project of Eastern Coalfield Limited, Lalmatia, Godda for 
considering the 84 workmen( as per list) engaged under contractors for the last 13 years for permanent absorptions in 
the company is not justified and so they are not entitled to the relief claimed. This reference is answered accordingly.

Organizing Secretary, Rashtriya Colliery Mazdoor Sangh, Dhanbad for adjudication by this Tribunal: 

SCHEDULE 

“Whether the action of the management of Bhuli Town Administration of M/s BCCL in not referring 

Sri Kanhaiya Lal, Accounts Asstt. To Apex Medical Board for assessment of his Physical debility till 

the date of his superannuation from service is justified? If not, to what relief is the concerned 

workman entitled ?” 
2. On receiving order no. L-20012/255/2002-IR(C-I) dated 24/12/2003 Government of India, Ministry of Labour,

2. The case of the workmen as per Written Statement filed on 07.07.2003 is that Jagdish Bhuia and other 


concerned workmen have been working as C.K. Section of Golukdih Colliery since 1991 continuously with 
unblemished record of service. The concerned workmen have been performing their job of Shale Picker, Coal 
Breaker, Wagon Levelling, Line Cleaning and other jobs since 1991 within the precinct and premises of the mines 
continuously. The concerned workmen have been performing permanent and perennial nature of job under the direct 
control and supervision of the management and the management also supplying all the implements for execution of 
jobs. The different collieries of the area have no railway siding such as Ghanoodih, Bera, Dobari, Bastacola GOCP 
etc and all the coal produced from the aforesaid collieries including Golukdih Colliery are being dispatched through 
railway siding which is situated at C.K. Section of Golukdih Colliery. The coal is extracted from the aforesaid 
collieries through solid blasting system and being transported to the C.K. Siding through dumper and the coals are 
unloaded thereto. It may not be out of place to mention that main function of the management is to raise coal from the 
collieries and to sell to the respective buyers and for the same the coal is dispatched through railway wagons. The 
management has already paid huge damages for not removing shale and other impurities from coal as the buyers are 
not ready to buy stones and other materials which are not coal. In view of the aforesaid fact the removal of shale and 
other impurities of coal is essentially required and that cannot be done through any machine and that can be done 
manually only. The concerned workmen have been rendering services and producing goods for the benefit of the 
management and they have rendered more than 240 days attendance in each year. In the coal industry the workmen 
are getting wages as per NCWA and the minimum category of a shale picker is Category-I. Though the management 
is public sector undertaking but unfortunately the management inspite of the aforesaid facts have been paying the 
concerned workmen wages below the rate of NCWA to deprive the concerned workmen and for that reason the 
management is disbursing their wages in the name of intermediary by posing them as alleged contractors. The 
disbursement of wages in the name of intermediary is nothing but a legal camouflage. The management have prepared 
and arranged all the paper arrangement to camouflage the real issue. To provide the concerned workmen of their 
legitimate wages and other facilities at par with permanent employees the management is not maintaining the 
statutory documents regarding the concerned workmen. The management always try to take advantage of their illegal 
act of non-maintaining statutory documents regarding the concerned workmen by submitting before the Tribunal that

the concerned workmen are not possessing appointment letter, Identity Card etc. As the management not paying the 
concerned workmen their legitimate wages and other facilities and not maintaining the statutory documents regarding 
their engagement for that reason the union raised the present case demanding regularization. The concerned workmen 
and the union on behalf of the concerned workmen have represented before the management several times for their 
regularization and at least for wages of Category-I as per NCWA but unfortunately the management did not take any 
cognizance of the same and in view of that after exhausting all avenues for amicable settlement the union raised 
industrial dispute demanding regularization of the concerned workmen but unfortunately the appropriate Government 
in utter violation of law laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in catena of cases rejected the dispute by an order 
dated 30.10.2000.The union challenged the illegal action of the appropriate Government before the Hon’ble 
Jharkhand High Court which was registered as CWJC No. 2016/2001 and on the basis of direction of the Hon’ble 
High Court the Government referred the dispute for adjudication with following schedule: 


“Whether the demand of Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union for regularization of Jagdish Bhuia and 119 others in 
Cat. I as per Annexure by the management of Bastacola Area of M/s. BCCL and for Cat. I wages as per NCWA is 
legal and justified? If yes, what relief the concerned workmen are entitled?” 


The demand for regularization of Jagdish Bhuia and 119 others and payment of Cat. I wages with 
retrospective effect are legal and justified. The action of the management of not regularizing the concerned workmen 
and not paying Cat. I wages as per NCWA was illegal, arbitrary, unjustified, discriminatory and against the principles 
of natural justice besides the same against the law of the land enunciated by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in catena of 
cases. The action of the management is malafide and vindictive and smacks of anti-labour policy of the management 
and at last it was prayed to answer the reference in favour of the workmen by directing the management to regularize 
the concerned workmen and to pay them wages as Cat. I with retrospective effect with all arrear of wages and 
consequential benefits. 


3. The case of the management as per the written statement cum rejoinder dated 10.02.2005 filed on behalf of 
the management is that the present reference is not maintainable either in law or in fact. No employer-employee 
relationship exists between the management and persons concerned. The sponsoring union raised the present 
industrial dispute and demanded regularization of Jagdish Bhuia and 119 others. The management have checked and 
verified the statutory records, such as Form ‘B’ Register, I.D. Card Register, Service Excerpt, Attendance Register, 
Payment Sheet etc. where none of the names of Jagdish Bhuia and others was found mentioned. It is relevant to

9. The Ld. Counsel for the union/workmen has submitted that all the concerned workmen of this reference case 


have been working at C.K. Section of Golukdih Colliery since 1991 continuously under the direct control and

management. The training certificates are not the certificate of being employees. They have no appointment letters, no 
identity cards etc. issued by the management and therefore, they are not the employees of the management rather they 
are the contractor’s employees and so they are not entitled for the relief of regularization and prayed to answer the

11. Issue 


“Whether the demand of Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union from the management of Bastacola Area of M/s. 
BCCL for regularization at least in Category-I of Sri Jagdish Bhuia and 119 other workmen as per list and payment of 
wages accordingly, is legal and justified? If so, to what relief the workmen concerned are entitled and from which 
date?” 


12. As regards the oral evidence, WW-1 Ashok Ram is one of the workmen and he has deposed that they have 
been working regularly and continuously as Shale Picker at C.K. Section of Golukdih Colliery since 1991-1992 under 
the direct control and supervision of the management. The different collieries of the areas have no railway siding such

Golukdih Colliery are being dispatched through C.K. Railway Siding. The coal is extracted through solid blasting 
system and so the stone and other impurities remain mixed with the produced coal. The coal so produced transported 
through dumpers and unloaded at C.K. Railway Siding. They have been performing the jobs of picking Shale from 
coal, picking and removing shale and other impurities from coal, wagon leveling, line cleaning, breaking coal into 
size and also removing shale from feeder breaker. The jobs that they have been performing are of permanent and

practical purposes they are the employees of the management but the management have been paying them below the 
rates of NCWA in the names of alleged intermediaries to camouflage the real issue and to exploit the poor workmen. 
The management has also given them vocational training and they have filed two items of documents namely 
Vocational Training Certificates marked as Exhibit W-1 series and Pay Slips marked as Exhibit W-2 series. As per

colliery for appointment. No appointment letter was issued to any workmen. No order was issued by the management 
to work as Shale Picker. They were not working under any contractor. He has not gone to underground mines though 
he has seen the collieries where production was done. The management was sending them to go to the different 
collieries but no order was issued to them for the same. He has denied that he has never worked with the management 
and have fabricated the documents. 


13. As regards the documentary evidence, Exhibit W-1 Series are the photo copies of Certificates in the name of 
all the concerned workmen issued on different dates in the year 2007 and it also transpires from the same that these 
concerned workmen have participated in the training program of safety of the contractor workers held at Regional 
Training Centre, Bastacola Area-IX under BCCL and it has been issued by the Regional Training Officer, Bastacola 
Area. Exhibit W-2 Series are the photo copies of pay sheets of the year 2002 that have been issued in the names of 
concerned workmen and it further transpires that these have been issued from the contractor Maa Lilori Transport Pvt. 
Ltd. Ckw Siding, Kujama and Ambey Mining Pvt. Ltd. CK Siding, Kujama, Bastacola-IX and all these pay 
sheets/slips are in the name of the workers with their designation as Shale Picker and account number, CMPF number 
as well as No. of days, Rate of wages, Basic pay, CMPF Amount, F.P Amount, SPL. Increment, H. Pay amount, 
Adv. amount, Total deduction and Net wages have also been mentioned. 


14. On the other hand the management has examined Prakash Kumar Mishra as MW-1 who has deposed that he 
was working as Personnel Manager at Golukdih Colliery since last one year. There is C.K. Siding but he has further 
deposed that they never engaged Shale Picker in C.K. Section and he has denied that Jagdish Bhuia and 119 others 
were engaged as Shale Picker in C.K. Area. He deposed that no contract was given for Shale Picking though 
transportation contract is given there. The contractor engaged their workmen and has further deposed that the 
regularizations of the workmen are not justified. In the cross-examination he has stated that there is no railway siding 
in Dobari Colliery, Bastacola Colliery etc. All coal raised from the colliery are loaded in wagon in C.K. Siding but he 
does not know whether the coal is raised by solid blasting. They separate Shale Coal from C.K. Railway siding but 
they cannot file any document for doing the job of Shale picking through their own workmen. He has also admitted 
that in all mines vocational rules are applicable and there is one vocational training centre in Bastacola Colliery. All 
the management’s employees were giving vocational training. He has denied that the workmen are working as Shale 
Picker since 1992 and their demand of regularization is justified. 


15. On perusal of the oral testimony of WW1 as also the statement of claim of the workmen it is evident that 
they have orally claimed that they have been working under the direct control and supervision of the management as 
shale picker since 1991-92 but they have failed to produce any documentary evidence such as attendance records, pay 
slips, order showing direct instruction from the principal employer, appointment letter, ID Cards etc directly issued 
from the management or witness statement from supervisor and proof that contractor lacked valid license or did not 
comply with statutory obligations etc. At the same time on perusal of Ext.W2 Series which are the photo copies of 
pay sheets/pay slips of different months of the year 2010 and 2011 that have been issued in the names of concerned 
workmen, it is self evident from these documents that these have been issued by the contractor Maa Lilori Transport 
Pvt. Ltd. Ckw Siding, Kujama and Ambey Mining Pvt. Ltd. CK Siding, Kujama, Bastacola-IX and not by the 
management which proves that these concerned workmen are the contractor’s workmen and supports the claim of the 
management that the concerned workmen are the contractor’s employees and they are not the employees of the 
management and also corroborates the oral testimony of MW1 that transportation contract is given there and the 
contractor engaged their workmen. 


Now as regards Ext.W1 Series, these prove that the workmen have participated in training program for the 
contractors labourers under BCCL for the purpose of safety but giving safety training to the concerned workmen do 
not by itself prove that they are the employees of the management because safety training is a legal obligation and not 
an employment benefit as under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970, the principal employer is 
responsible for ensuring the health and safety of all workers on their premises including contract labourers. Providing 
safety training and personal protective equipment is a statutory requirement to prevent accidents and exploitation and 
not a proof of employer-employee relationship. Not only this, the workmen have also failed to adduce any cogent 
evidence to prove their claim that the contractors have been interposed only to camouflage the real issue. 


As regards the authority cited by the learned advocate of the workmen reported in 2011 LLR 1079, in this 
case the workmen were working under the order of the officers of the employer whereas in the instant case the 
workmen have failed to bring on record any such order or direction of the principal employer rather the copies of pay 
slips submitted by them clearly show the names of their contractors as Maa Lilori Transport Pvt. Ltd and Ambey 


7372 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 6, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 15, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Mining Pvt. Ltd proving that they were working under them and thus the facts and circumstances of the instant case 
are different from the cited case and so can not be applied in the instant case and same is the situation with the other 
one. 


Thus on the basis of the above appreciation of the facts, circumstances and evidence available on the case 
record this Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the concerned workmen have failed to prove their case that they are 
the employees of the management and not the contractor’s employees and so they are not legally entitled to 
regularization in Category-1 and accordingly it is held that the demand of Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union from the 
management of Bastacola Area of M/s. BCCL for regularization at least in Category-I of Sri Jagdish Bhuia and 119 
other workmen as per list and payment of wages accordingly, is neither reasonable nor justified and so they are not 
entitled to get any relief as claimed. The Reference is answered accordingly.

Exhibit M-3 it transpires that this is enquiry notice dated 21.01.2003 by which Sri B.R. Shukla, Senior Personnel 
Officer, Burragarh Colliery, appointed as Enquiry Officer directed Gurupado Bauri to appear on 17.02.2003 at 10 AM 
in the office of manager Burragarh colliery and he was also informed that he will be given full opportunity to defend 
himself in course of enquiry and if he wishes to appear with a co-worker, he will be allowed for the same also and if 
he failed to appear, the enquiry will be done Ex-parte. On perusal of Exhibit M-4 it transpires that this is copy of 
enquiry proceeding held against the workman Gurupado Bauri from 17.02.03 to 14.03.03 in pursuance of the charge 
sheet dated 18/19.11.2002. On its careful perusal it transpires that during course of proceeding on 17.02.03, 01.03.03 
and 14.03.03 the charge sheeted workman remained absent even after due notice/information and so the enquiry 
commenced ex parte. Thereafter the statement of management representative Sri B-R. Singh was recorded in which he 
has elaborately stated regarding the misconduct of the workman for his unauthorized absence from duty since 
01.11.02 and after charge sheet he neither submitted any show cause nor appeared during enquiry proceeding. He also 
described his past misconduct record of unauthorized absence from duty since 9.04.2001 for which he was punished 
after charge sheet and enquiry with stoppage of 2 SPRA. Exhibit M-5 is the enquiry report signed by Sr. EO/Sr. P.O, 
Burragarh Colliery and on its perusal it transpires that during enquiry the charge of unauthorized absence of 
Gurupado Bouri from duty since 01.11.2002 was found proved. Exhibit M-6 is the second show cause notice dated 
20/24.03.03 issued to the workman Sri Gurupado Bouri by which he was informed that he was found guilty during 
enquiry against him and so he was being given another opportunity to submit his comment in his defence within 7 
days of the receipt of this notice failing which management will take appropriate action in this matter. Exhibit M-7 is 
the Note sheet dated 02.04.2003 and on its perusal it is evident that full details of Gurupado Bouri, Miner Loader of 
Burragarh Colliery such as the name, designation, personnel no., date of appointment, date of birth, date and period of 
unauthorized absence, date of charge sheet, finding on charge, last three years attendance, recommendation of the 
manager, past punishment by stoppage of 2 SPRA etc have been fully mentioned. Exhibit M-8_ is the Dismissal 
Order dated 30.04.2003 and on its perusal it is evident that it has been issued to Sri Gurupado Bouri informing that in 
view of the enquiry report of the enquiry conducted on the charge of his unauthorized absence from duty since 
01.11.2002 as well as considering his past record which were aggravating, Burragarh Colliery came to the conclusion 
to dismiss him from the services of the management with immediate effect. 


12. Thus, on the basis of above discussions of the documentary evidences adduced from the side of the 
management it is established that the workman Gurupado Bouri who was working as Miner Loader in Burragarh 
Colliery, absented himself from his duty since 01.11.2002 without any information or leave from the competent 
authority and thereafter he was issued charge sheet on 18/19.11.2002 under clause 26.1.1 of the certified standing 
order of the coal mining industry for willful and habitual absence from duty and was directed to show cause within 48 
hours of the receipt of charge sheet but he did not submit his show cause, so domestic enquiry proceeding was started 
against him in which also he did not appear even after due notice on 3 dates so the enquiry was conducted ex parte 
and ultimately he was found guilty of absenting himself from his duty since 01.11.2002 without prior permission and 
leave of the competent authority that the union also admitted by filing a petition dated 12.02.2020. Not only this, the 
materials on record further reveal that the attendance of the workman in the past three years from 2000 to 2002 is not 
satisfactory and previously also he remained absent from his duty without giving any information to the competent 
authority since 09.04.2001for which he was punished by stoppage of two SPRA because of being absent 
unauthorisedly from duty since 09.04.2001. 


13. Thus the above materials establish that the workman is a habitual absentee and for habitual absentee, the 
penalty of dismissal is quite justified because a prior penalty like stoppage of 2 SPRA indicates that the employee was 
already warned about the seriousness of the unauthorized absence from duty. Therefore, a repeated misconduct 
demonstrates lack of improvement and a disregard for workplace rules and proceedings which can be seen as an 


7376 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 6, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 15, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


aggravating factor in a domestic proceeding making dismissal a more plausible outcome. Complete absence from 
enquiry proceeding as well as not submitting any show cause/reply goes to prove the workman’s disrespect towards 
the established system as well as procedure of the institution where he was working so no mitigating circumstance 
any more is visible in this case. 


In case of Om Prakash Vs State of Punjab & Ors reported in (2011) 14 SCC 682, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has been pleased to hold that habitual absentee without leave does not deserve any sympathy from the court. 


14. Now as regards the contention of the learned representative of the workman that the dismissal of the 
workman Gurupado Bouri from the services of the company is harsh and disproportionate in view of his misconduct, 
is not tenable in the eye of law because the Hon’ble Apex Court in case of Maan Singh vs Union of India, reported 
in AIR 2003 supreme court 1800, has been pleased to hold that habitual absenteeism without leave is sufficient to 
provide major punishment of dismissal. 


15. Now as regards the contention of the Ld. Representative of the workman that the workman can not be 
imposed major penalty if charge sheet has been issued under clause 26.1.1 of Certified Standing Order of coal mining 
industry and the workman has been allowed only 48 hours to show cause which indicates minor penalty, though this 
is settled principle of law that a workman can not be punished for a charge not included in the charge sheet but if the 
past misconduct of the workman has been brought on record in the enquiry report, major punishment can be imposed 
in view of past and present repeated misconduct. In this regard, the Hon’ble Apex Court has been pleased to hold in 
case of state of Punjab & Ors. Vs. Ex. C. Satpal Singh, Civil Appeal No. 312/2012 reported in INSC 1056 and 
delivered on 29.08.2025, that the “past misconduct cannot be the basis for punishment unless it is cited in the show- 
cause notice or inquiry report. 


Here in the instant case on perusal of the case record it transpires that though the past misconduct of the 
unauthorized absence of the workman Gurupado Bouri has not been mentioned in the show cause notice but on 
perusal of the enquiry proceeding Exhibit (M-4) it is crystal clear that the past misconduct of Gurupado Bouri has 
been very clearly mentioned therein and therefore, the contention of the Ld. Representative of the workman that the 
charge sheet was issued for minor punishment and therefore, the major punishment cannot be imposed is not legally 
tenable in the eye of law and considering the past misconduct as well as the present misconduct it is crystal clear that 
the workman is a habitual absentee for which action of the management of Burragarh Colliery of M/s. BCCL in 
dismissing the workman Sri Gurupado Bouri from the services of the company w.e.f. 30.04.2003 is held justified and 
accordingly the workman is not entitled to any relief. So this issue is decided against the workman and the reference 
is answered accordingly.

New Delhi for information and notification.

As per letter dated 11/05/2017 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per 
Notification No. L-22012/88/2016 (IR(CM-ID) dt. 11/05/2017. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action on the part of the management of Sub Area Manager, Surakachhar Colliery of 
SECL, Korba Area, Distt. Korba (CG) and appeal rejected by the Management of SECL Headquarter, 
Bilaspur in not considering towards reinstatement of service with back wages in respect of Shri Sitaram 
Banjare, S/o Ghurau Banjare, Ex-Pump Khalasi w.e.f. 13/12/2005 is legal, appropriate and justified? If 
not, to what relief Shri Sitaram Banjare, the delinquent workman is entitled to?” 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


Case of the Workman, is mainly that when he was posted as Pump Khalasi, SECL Balgi Project, he was 
issued a charge sheet dated 15.11.2004, with an allegation of misconduct with regard to misbehavior with Officers 
and threatened them thus, committing misconduct under Clause 26.16, 26.18 & 26.22 and Certified Standing Orders. 


It is further his case that the management failed to follow principles of natural justice during the course of 
inquiry, proceeded ex-parte against the workman and conducted inquiry without affording sufficient and proper 
opportunity to the workman , the enquiry officer wrongly concluded that the charges were proved and the punishment 
was also disproportionate to the charges proved. 


The case of management is that, while the workman was working on 13.11.2004 as Pump Khalasi, 
Category-III, he assaulted Shri U.S. Goyal and P.L. Kewat who were Superintendent of Mines in Balgi Project. He 
was issued a charge-sheet containing charges of misconduct under Clause 26.16, 26.18 and 26.22 of the Certified 
Standing Orders on 15.11.2004. He submitted his reply on 27.11.2004. On finding the reply unsatisfactory, 
management decided to conduct regular departmental inquiry. The inquiry concluded in as many as 20 sittings in 
which the workman was given full opportunity to defend himself. The Disciplinary Authority issued show cause 
notice against him. Another show cause notice was issued by Appellate Authority at appeal stage asking the workman 
to show cause with respect to inquiry and punishment. The workman did submit his reply and thereafter punishment 
order was passed and confirmed, the management has also pleaded that the charges were rightly held proved and 
punishment is also not disproportionate to the charges proved. 


Following preliminary issue was framed on the basis of pleadings. 
Whether the departmental enquiry conducted against the workman is just, proper and legal? 


This issue was decided after evidence vide order dated 03.10.2024, the departmental enquiry was held not 
vitiated in law. This order is part of this Judgment. 


Following Additional Issues were framed, thereafter:- 
1. Whether finding of the enquiry officer that the charges are proved can be held perverse? 
2. Whether the punishment awarded is disproportionate to the charges proved? 

Parties were given opportunity to lead evidence on additional issues, they proposed no evidence. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for the workman Mr. Arun Patel, and Learned Senior Counsel 
Mr. Anoop Nair, assisted by Learned Counsel Mr. Neeraj Kewat for Management. I have gone through the record as 
well. 


Additional Issue No. 1- 


The charges against the workman are mainly that on 30.11.2004 at about 01:00 pm, the workman came in the 
O/o MTK of 1 & 2 Mine and abused Shri U.S. Goyal, Superintendent of Mines saying that he did not award duty to 
the workman and also alleging that he accepted bribe. It is further alleged that the workman threatened Shri U.S. 
Goyal to kill him and assaulted him as well beat him by Chappal, thus, committing misconduct under Clause 26.16, 
26.18 & 26.22 of the Certified Standing Orders. 


Perusal of enquiry papers reveals that the workman has not denied his presence at the time, place and date of 
the incident. He has also stated before the enquiry officer that infact, he was forced to bribe Shri U.S. Goyal which he 
paid, Shri U.S. Goyal was demanding more money, for this he himself abused the workman and it was only on this 
provocation, the workman abused him. The workman denied the allegations that he assaulted Shri U.S. Goyal and 
also that he was drunk at that time. He also denied the words he is alleged to have used in abuse against 
Shri U.S. Goyal. 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : दिसम्बर 6, 2025/ अग्रहायण 15, 1947 7381 


Management has examined witnesses on fact which have corroborated the charges. These witnesses have not 
deposed in their cross-examination that Shri U.S. Goyal also abused the workman. The case that the workman 
misbehaved or abused Shri U.S. Goyal on provocation by him is to be proved by the workman himself, except his 
statement before the enquiry officer, there is no evidence in form of any eye witness to the incident to support his 
case. On the contrary, the victim and the eye witness examined have corroborated the case of management. 


Scope of disciplinary proceedings and scope of criminal proceedings are quite distinct, exclusive and 
independent of each other. Standards of proof in the two proceedings are also different. Ref. T.N.C.S. Corpn. Ltd. vs. 
K. Meerabai, (2006) 2 SCC 255 


Standard of proof in a departmental enquiry which is quasicriminal/quasi-judicial in nature: Disciplinary 
proceedings, however, being quasi-criminal in nature, there should be some evidence to prove the charge(emphasis 
supplied). Although the charges in a departmental proceedings are not required to be proved like a criminal trial i.e. 
beyond all reasonable doubts, we cannot lose sight of the fact that the enquiry officer performs a quasi judicial 
function, who upon analyzing the documents must arrive at a conclusion that there had been a preponderance of 
probability to prove the charges on the basis of materials on record. While doing so, he cannot take into 
consideration any irrelevant fact. He cannot refuse to consider the relevant facts. He cannot shift the burden of proof. 
He cannot reject the relevant testimony of the witnesses only on the basis of surmises and conjectures. Ref: (i) 
Nirmala J. Jhala Vs. State of Gujarat & Another, AIR 2013 SC 1513 (paras 10, 11, 12 & 13). (ii) M.V. Bijlani Vs. 
Union of India, (2006) 5 SCC 88 (Para 25) 


In the cases of (i) NOIDA Entrepreneurs Association Vs NOIDA & others, AIR 2007 SC 1161 (i4i) State 
Bank of India Vs. R.B. Sharma, (2004) 7 SCC 27 (iii) Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan Vs. T. Srinivas, (2004) 7 
SCC 442 (iv) Depot Manager, APSRTC Vs. Mohd. Yousuf Miya, (1997) 2 SCC 699 (v) Captain M. Paul Anthony 
Vs. Bharat Gold Mines Limited (1999) 3 SCC 679 and (vi) State of Rajasthan Vs. B.K. Meena, (1996) 6 SCC 417 
(vi) Pratap Singh Vs. State of Punjab, AIR 1964 SC 72 (vii) Jang Bahadur Singh Vs. Baij Nath, AIR 1969 SC 30, 
it has been laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that "the purpose of departmental enquiry and of prosecution are 
two different and distinct aspects. Departmental Enquiry is to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of 
public service. Crime is an act of commission in violation of law or of omission of public duty. The enquiry in a 
departmental proceeding relates to the conduct or breach of duty by the delinquent officer to punish him for his 
misconduct defined under the relevant statutory rules or law. It is the settled legal position that the strict standard of 
proof or applicability of the Evidence Act stands excluded in a departmental proceeding. Criminal Proceedings and 
the departmental proceeding under enquiry can go on simultaneously." 


In the case of T.N.C.S. Corporation Ltd. Vs. K. Meerabai, (2006) 2 SCC 255, it has been held by the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court that the scopes of the disciplinary proceedings and of criminal proceedings are quite distinct, 
exclusive and independent of each other. Standards of proof in the two proceedings are also different. 


In the cases of Mohd. Saleem Siddiqui Vs. State of UP & others, (2011) 2 UPLBEC 1575 (Allahabad High 
Court) and Ajeet Kumar Naag Vs. General Manager Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. Haldia, JT 2005 (8) SC 425, the 
distinction between departmental enquiry and criminal proceedings has been drawn as under: "The two proceedings 
i.e. criminal and departmental are entirely different. They operate in different fields and have different objectives. The 
object of criminal proceedings is to inflict appropriate punishment on offender and the purpose of enquiry 
proceedings is to deal with the delinquent departmentally and to impose penalty in accordance service rules the rule 
relating to appreciation of evidence in the two proceedings is also not similar. In criminal law burden of proof is on 
the prosecution and unless the prosecution is able to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubts, he cannot 
be convicted by a court of law. In departmental enquiry, on the other hand, penalty can be imposed on the delinquent 
officer on a finding recorded on the basis of preponderance of probability. Procedure with respect to standard of proof 
in criminal case and departmental enquiry are different. In the case of departmental enquiry the technical rules of 
evidence have no application and the doctrine of "proof beyond doubt" has also no application in the departmental 
enquiry. Criminal prosecution is launched for an offence for violation of a duty the offender owes to the society or for 
breach of which law has provided that the offender shall make satisfaction to the public. So crime is an act of 
commission in violation of law or of omission of public duty. The departmental enquiry is to maintain discipline in the 
service and efficiency of public service. There would be no bar to proceed simultaneously with departmental enquiry 
and trial of criminal case. " 


Now testing the aforesaid evidence on the parameters led down above, the finding of enquiry officer that the 
charges are proved cannot be held to be perverse. 

Additional Issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. 

Additional Issue No. 2. 

The charges proved the workman has misbehaved and physically assaulted as well abused on his senior 


officer is lack of discipline. Learned Counsel for management has relied on judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in 
the case, Civil Appeal No. 1508 of 2003, Mahindra and Mahindra v/s NB Narwade, 2005 (3) SCC 134. In this case, 


7382 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 6, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 15, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


it has been held that in case of acts subversive of discipline, and use of abusive language to senior officer, punishment 
of dismissal may be awarded. 


Learned Counsel for workman has attempted to distinguish the judgment with an argument that in the 
referred judgment, the workman had several acts of same misconduct behind him committed by him, which is not in 
the case in hand, case thus was the first misconduct proved against the workman. Management has referred to another 
judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case, Civil Appeal No. 881 of 2006, L. K. Verma v/s H.M.T. Ltd. & Anr. 
2006 (2) SCC 269, in which verbal abuse is held to be sufficient for punishment of dismissal, case of Mahindra and 
Mahindra (supra) has also been referred to in this judgment. It has been observed in this case that verbal abuse has 
been held to be sufficient for inflicting the punishment of dismissal, Hon’ble Supreme Court also observed that the 
workman in the referred case had admitted that he verbally abused his senior but his conduct never showed that he 
had any remorse. 


Learned Counsel for workman has submitted that the punishment is disproportionate to the charges because 
otherwise, the service record of the workman has been spotless, the disciplinary authority and appellate authority did 
not consider this fact. He has referred to the judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court reported in AIR (1964) 364, in 
which, it has been held that only suspension will not amount to proof. This judgment has been followed by Hon’ble 
High Court of M.P. in the case reported in 2003 (1) MPLJ 487. 


Learned Counsel has further referred to another judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Union 
of India v/s J. Ahmad, AIR (1979) SC 1022, which defines misconduct and lays down that innocent mistakes do not 
constitute misconduct. Learned counsel has referred to another judgment of The Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case 
of Inspector Premchand v/s Government of NCT Delhi (2007) 4 SCC 566, in which the same law has been 
approved. 


The settled proposition of law is that the punishment can be interfered by this Tribunal only when it is so 
disproportionate to the charge that it shocks the conscience of this Tribunal. Following judgments are being referred 
to in this respect. 


Hon’ble Apex Court in B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India, (1995) 6 SCC 749 while discussing about the 
scope of judicial review, in disciplinary matters, has observed as under: 


“The High CourvTribunal, while exercising the power of judicial review, cannot normally substitute its 
own conclusion on penalty and impose some other penalty. If the punishment imposed by the disciplinary 
authority or the appellate authority shocks the conscience of the High Court/Tribunal, it would 
appropriately mold the relief, either directing the disciplinary/appellate authority to reconsider the penalty 
imposed, or to shorten the litigation, it may itself, in exceptional and rare cases, imposed appropriate 
punishment with cogent reasons in support thereof.” 


In DG, RPF vs. Sai Babu (2003) 4 SCC 331, Hon’ble Apex Court has observed that: 


“Osssevausunets Normally, the punishment imposed by a disciplinary authority should not be disturbed by the 
High Court or a tribunal except in appropriate cases that too only after reaching a conclusion that the 
punishment imposed is grossly or shockingly disproportionate, after examining all the relevant factors 
including the nature of charges proved against, the past conduct, penalty imposed earlier, the nature of 
duties assigned having due regard to their sensitiveness, exactness expected of an discipline required to be 
maintained, and the department/establishment which the delinquent person concerned works.” 


In United Commercial Bank vs. P.C. Kakkar (2003) 4 SCC 364 Hon’ble Apex Court on review of a long 
line of cases and the principles of judicial review of administrative action under English law summarized the legal 
position in the following words: 


“11. The common thread running through in all these decisions is that the court should not interfere 
with the administrators’ decision unless it was illogical or suffers from procedural impropriety or was 
shocking to the conscience of the court, in the sense that it was in defiance of logic or moral standards. 
In view of what has been stated in Wednesbury case the court would not go into the correctness of the 
choice made by the administrator open to him and the court should not substitute its decision to that of the 
administrator. The scope of judicial review is judicial review is limited to the deficiency in decision- 
making process and not the decision. 


12. To put it differently, unless the punishment imposed by the disciplinary authority or the appellate 
authority shocks the conscience of the court/tribunal, there is no scope for interference. Further, to 
shorten litigation it may, in exceptional and rare cases, impose appropriate punishment by recording 
cogent reasons in support thereof.” 


In Union of India vs. S.S. Ahluwalia (2007) 7 SCC 257 Hon’ble Supreme Court reiterated the legal position 
as follows: 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : दिसम्बर 6, 2025/ अग्रहायण 15, 1947 7383 


260, , बेर The scope of judicial review in the matter of imposition of penalty as a result of 
disciplinary proceedings is very limited. The court can interfere with the punishment only if it finds the 
same to be shockingly disproportionate to the charges found to be proved.” 

In State of Meghalaya v. Mecken Singh N. Marak (2008) 7 SCC 580 Hon’ble Supreme Court stated that: 

“The punishment imposed by the disciplinary authority or the appellate authority unless 
shocking to the conscience of the court, cannot be subjected to judicial review. 

Hon’ble Apex Court in Administrator, UnionTerritory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli vs. Gulbhia M. Lad 
(2010) 2 SCC (L&S) 101 has observed that 

“The legal position is fairly well settled that while exercising the power of judicial review, the 
High Court or a Tribunal cannot interfere with the discretion exercised by the disciplinary authority, 
and/or on appeal the appellate authority with regard to the imposition of punishment unless such 
discretion suffers from illegality or material procedural irregularity or that would shock the conscience of 
the court/tribunal. The exercise of discretion in imposition of punishment by the disciplinary authority or 
appellate authority is dependent on host of factors such as gravity of misconduct, past conduct, the nature 
of duties assigned to the delinquent, responsibility of the position that the delinquent holds, previous 
penalty, if any, and the discipline required to be maintained in the department or establishment he works. 
Ordinarily the court or the tribunal would not substitute its opinion on reappraisal of facts. 

This extract is taken from State Bank of Bikaner & Jaipur v. Nemi Chand Nalwaya, (2011) 4 SCC 584 : 
(2011) 1 SCC (L&S) 721 : 2011 SCC OnLine SC 416 at page 587 

7. It is now well settled that the courts will not act as an appellate court and reassess the evidence led in 

the domestic enquiry, nor interfere on the ground that another view is possible on the material on record. 

If the enquiry has been fairly and properly held and the findings are based on evidence, the question of 

adequacy of the evidence or the reliable nature of the evidence will not be grounds for interfering with the 

findings in departmental enquiries. Therefore, courts will not interfere with findings of fact recorded in 
departmental enquiries, except where such findings are based on no evidence or where they are clearly 
perverse. The test to find out perversity is to see whether a tribunal acting reasonably could have arrived 
at such conclusion or finding, on the material on record. The courts will however interfere with the 
findings in disciplinary matters, if principles of natural justice or statutory regulations have been violated 
or if the order is found to be arbitrary, capricious, mala fide or based on extraneous considerations. 

(Vide B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India [(1995) 6 SCC 749 : 1996 SCC (L&S) 80 : (1996) 32 ATC 44] 

+ Union of India v. G. Ganayutham [(1997) 7 SCC 463 : 1997 SCC (L&S) 1806] , Bank of India v. Degala 

Suryanarayana [(1999) 5 SCC 762 : 1999 SCC (L&S) 1036] and High Court of Judicature at 

Bombay v. Shashikant S. Patil [(2000) 1 SCC 416 : 2000 SCC (L&S) 144] .) 

In Air India Corporation Bombay vs. V.A. Ravellow 1972 (25) FLR 319 (SC) it has been observed that: 

“Once the employer has lost the confidence in the employee and the bona fide loss of confidence 
is affirmed, the order of punishment must be considered to be immune from challenge, for the reason that 
discharging the office of trust and confidence requires absolute integrity, and in a case of loss of 
confidence, reinstatement cannot be directed.” 

In Knhaiyalal Agarwal and others vs. Factory Manager, Gwaliar Sugar Co. Ltd. AIR 2001 SC 3645 
Hon’ble Apex Court laid down the test for loss of confidence to find out as to whether there was bona fide loss of 
confidence in the employee, observing that: 

“Loss of confidence cannot be subjective, based upon the mind of the management. Objective facts which 
would lead to a definite inference of apprehension in the mind of the management, regarding trust worthiness or 
reliability of the employee, must be alleged and proved.” 

Abuse and physical assault by a subordinate against his superior becomes a more serious matter. It is not a 
quarrel between two equal persons who are equally placed, such type of misconduct if permitted, will be subversive to 
discipline, no establishment can run without discipline, which is the core of an establishment. In this circumstance, 
the action of management in awarding punishment of dismissal to the workman from service is held to be not so 
shockingly disproportionate to invite interference of this Tribunal. 

Hence, holding the punishment not disproportionate to the charges proved. 

Additional Issue No. 2 is answered accordingly. 

On the basis of above discussion and findings, the reference deserves to be answered as follows:- 
AWARD 

Holding the action on the part of the management of Sub Area Manager, Surakachhar Colliery of SECL, 
Korba Area, Distt. Korba (CG) and appeal rejected by the Management of SECL Headquarter, Bilaspur in not 
considering towards reinstatement of service with back wages in respect of Shri Sitaram Banjare, w.e.f. 13/12/2005 
legal, appropriate and justified, the workman is held entitled to no relief.” 

No order as to cost.
