recruitment exercise on account of overage; that discriminatory or selective regularisation allegations lack foundation; 
and that consecutive rejection by the courts of his claims illustrates that the current dispute lacks merit and is barred in 
law. On these grounds, the management prayed for dismissal of the claim. 


13. It is also important to mention here that, as per the record from the Labour Commissioner, Assistant Labour 
Commissioner, Ms. Sakshi Chugh, while dealing with the claim of the claimant, has opined that further reference for 
adjudication in the present dispute is against the principle of res judicata, as enunciated by the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court in the matter of Chairman and Managing Director, The Fertilizers and Chemicals Travancore Ltd. & Anr. 
vs. General Secretary FACT Employees Association & Ors. (Civil Appeal No. 3803/2019), considering the fact that 
matter has attained finality after the dismissal of the SLP preferred by the claimant against the order of the Hon’ble 
High Court of Delhi. However, despite this, the matter has been referred to this Tribunal for fresh adjudication on the 
ground that the Central Government is the appropriate authority. 


14. Considering the fact that the same matter between the same parties has already attained finality, the principle 
of res judicata is applicable in the present case. Moreover, it would be a waste of time for this Tribunal to allow the 
matter to be contested again, because of the fact that matter has already been adjudicated before the competent Labour 
Courts of the Government of Delhi, where this matter was filed earlier. It was the management that raised the 
objection regarding lack of jurisdiction. However, instead of withdrawing the claim, the claimant preferred to 
continue the proceedings before the appropriate Court/Tribunal. Therefore, he has assumed the jurisdiction of that 
Court. Moreover, if the petition is allowed to continue, the evidence would be the same which had been led before the 
earlier Courts/Tribunal. Entertaining the same dispute again would amount to waste of the valuable time of this 
Tribunal. 


15. In view of the above discussion, claim is not maintainable as it is barred by the principles of res judicata. 
Hence, claim stands dismissed. Award is passed accordingly. A copy of this award is sent to appropriate government 
for notification under section 17 of the I.D. Act. File is consigned to record room.

AWARD

1. This is an application under section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 


“the Act”) filed by the claimant stating that he was appointed by the management as Assistant Station Manager on 
01.09.2009 and posted to IGI Airport Terminal-3. He worked with the management diligently and honestly and 
sincerely to the entire satisfaction of the managements and has never given any chance for complaint. He was illegally 
terminated on 21.01.2014 without assigning any reason which is a violation of section 25F of the ID Act. He has gone 
to the conciliation officer. During the course of conciliation before ALC, Delhi on last date i.e. 07.11.2014, 
management fraudulently and mischievously produced fabricated documents and obtained false complaints against 
him. Hence, he filed the present claim with the prayer that he be reinstated with full back wages. 


2. Management has filed the reply/written statement. He has taken various preliminary objections, stating that 
claimant is not the “workman” within the provision of the Industrial Disputes Act; present case is not maintainable, as 
the respondent does not fall under the definition of “management” within the Act; present claim is not maintainable as 
there is no industrial disputes arises; present claim is not maintainable as the services of the workman was terminated 
in accordance with the terms and conditions stipulated in the appointment letter dated 26.08.2009. He further 
submitted that the last drawn salary of the workman was Rs. 45,000/- per month. He submitted that a lot of 
complaints received against the claimant regarding his behavior. He submitted that claim be dismissed. 


3. After completion of the pleadings vide order dated 01.07.2015, following issues have been framed: 

(1) Whether claimant is workman as per provisions of section 2(s) of the ID Act? If so, its effect? 

(1) Whether there is industrial Disputes between the parties under the provisions of Industrial Disputes? If so, its 
effect? 


(1) Whether the services of Sh. Nitin Kohli were illegally terminated by management? If so, its effect? 


(IV) Whether the workman Sh. Nitin Kohli was not gainfully employed after alleged termination of him/after 
leaving services of the respondent as alleged by management? If so, its effect? 


(V) Whether the workman is entitled to be reinstated with full back wages and all consequential benefits 
alongwith cost? 


4. Matter is listed for cross-examination of the workman. Despite repeated opportunities, no one appeared on 
behalf of the management to cross-examine the workman. 


D5 I have gone through the record and found that, this case has been listed for arguments since 02.07.2025, on 
the maintainability of the claim, in view of the preliminary objections raised by the management regarding status of 
the workman. According to the management, claimant does not fall within the definition of the “workman” as defined 
under section 2(s) of the Act. However, since July, 2025, claimant was given three opportunities to advance his 
argument for clarification on the maintainability of his claim, but he is not appearing for arguing the matter, even 
today, after availing three opportunities. 


7450 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 13, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 22, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


6. It is also the matter of fact that the claimant has tried to amend the claim after framing of issues, by stating 
that he was designated as an Assistant Station Manager, however, the designation of manager was merely a Sham or 
Camouflage. He was having no managerial, administrative or supervisory powers and was a workman within the 
meaning of Section 2(S) of the ID Act. His application was rejected by this Tribunal, so, the claimant cannot say that 
he was not the Assistant Station Manager at that time. 


7. To invoke the jurisdiction of this tribunal, first the claimant has to assert that he was a workman within the 
definition of Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Section 2(s) is required to be reproduced herein: 


2 [(s) “workman” means any person (including an apprentice) employed in any industry to do any manual, 
unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, whether the terms 
of employment be express or implied, and for the purposes of any proceeding under this Act in relation to an 
industrial dispute, includes any such person who has been dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection 
with, or as a consequence of, that dispute, or whose dismissal, discharge or retrenchment has led to that 
dispute, but does not include any such person— 


(i) who is subject to the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950), or the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950), or the Navy 
Act, 1957 (62 of 1957); or 

(ii) who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison; or 

(iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity; or (iv) who, being employed ina 
supervisory capacity, draws wages exceeding 3 [ten thousand rupees] per mensem or exercises, either by the 
nature of the duties attached to the office or by reason of the powers vested in him, functions mainly of a 
managerial nature.] 


8. Definition of the workman as provided U/s 2(s) is wide enough to include any person as workman in respect 
of his earning; however, section has itself carved out the exception as Clause-(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv). Clause-(iii) 
specifically debarred the person, claiming to a workman if he is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative 
capacity. 


9. In this regard, the appointment issued on 26.08.2009 is important. In the said appointment letter, it has been 
mentioned that claimant was appointed by the management as Assistant Airport Manager, at IGI Airport 
Terminal-II, New Delhi-110037. He was given the salary of Rs. 40,000/- per month. It was also mentioned in his 
salary slip that he can be terminated any time on 7 days notice on either side. 


10. In the order dated 17.04.2025, he himself admitted in response to the court query that he had completed his 
Master’s degree in Tourism Management in 2006 and his job was to manage the affairs at the site. He also stated 
before this Tribunal that he had been supervising three employees at that time. 


11. All these facts establish that the claimant is not the “workman” as defined under section 2(s) of the ID Act. 
Hence, his claim stands dismissed. Award is passed accordingly. A copy of this award is sent to the appropriate 
government for notification as required under section 17 of the 1.7 Act, 1947. Record of this file is consigned to 
record room.

3: The substance of the claim petition is that the II Party/Management maintains two different conditions of

8.33% restricted to salary ceiling and payment ceiling and announced small amount of ex-gratia and it was revised

contract labourers are not only entitled to same wages and allowances and other benefits on the “principle of equal

14. Heard the learned counsels appeared on either side and perused the records. The question that arises for 


consideration is whether the contract labourers is entitled to get maximum bonus @ 20% of the salary/wages and ex- 
gratia? 


15. The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 provides statutory rights to employees to claim bonus. The minimum 
bonus as per section 10 of the Act is payable to@ 8.33% and as per section 31A of the Act, it shall not exceed 20% 
of salary/wages of the employee. 


16. The Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 1970, provides for registration and licensing in case 
one employs more than 20 contract labourers in the organization. This Act also provides various rights to the contract 
labourers such as to get wages, overtime wages and allowances, according to Minimum Wages Act. Section 8 of the 
Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 1970, provides that any employee who has worked for 30 days or 
more shall be entitled to get bonus from the employer. Now the question arises is that who is liable to pay bonus 
and ex-gratia to contract labourers. Admittedly, the Respondent is paying bonus to the contract labourers also @ 
8.33%, but, the Claimant union claims that bonus to be paid @ 20% along with ex-gratia. 


17. In the case of J.K.Ginning & Pressing Factory Vs. P.O Second Labour Court, Akola & Others, where the 
factory had employed 10 seasonal workers and the question arose as to their eligibility for bonus, wherein the 
Hon’ble Bombay High Court held that Act does not exclude such seasonal workers. In the case of Arun Mills Ltd. 
Vs Dr.Chandra Parshad C.Trivedi (1976) 32 FLR 323, it was held that employees working on a part-time basis are 
eligible for bonus. In light of the above judgements, it may be concluded that contract labourers also entitled to get 
bonus. Simply the question remains who is liable to pay bonus to contract labourers. 


18. In the case of Cominco Binanao Zinc vs Pappachand (1989) 1 LLJ 452, a factory had hired contract 
laboureres to run the management canteen. The dispute arose regarding payment of bonus to contractual laboureres, 
wherein the Hon’ble Kerala High Court held that contractual labour does not become employee of the company 
merely because they were managing canteen on behalf of the management and as per section 21(4) of the Contract 
Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 1970, principal employer is liable to pay arrears of wages, however, wages do 
not include gratuity and bonus and thus, held that principle employer cannot be held to be liable to pay bonus to 
contract workers. 


[भाग त--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : दिसम्बर 13, 2025/अग्रहायण 22, 1947 7457 


19. In the case of Kerala State Civil Supplies Corporation Vs Industrial Tribunal (2007) (I) KLJ 522, the 
Appellant a PSU had hired contractual labour and no bonus was paid to these workers on the ground that Bonus Act 
does not include contractual labour. The Hon’ble Court held that workers do not fall within the definition of 
employees under the Bonus Act. 


20. In the case of Shachindra Kumar Vs. State of Karnataka (2013) LLR 595 (Kar HC), where the labour 
department penalized the factory on the ground that contractual labour was not paid bonus equal to regular 
employees of the company. In this case, the contract labourers were paid minimum bonus as per section 10 of the 
Payment of Bonus Act. The labour department demanded that contract labour should be paid bonus at par with the 
regular employees as per provisions of section 11 of the Act. The Hon’ble Court held that contract labour cannot 
be treated on par with the regular employees for the purpose of payment of bonus and the Court quashed the 
proceedings against the factory and stated that when contract labourers are not employees as defined under 
Payment of Bonus Act, there is no obligation on the part of the employer to pay bonus on par with the regular 
employees. 


21. Thus, the above judgements clearly describe that contractual employees will not be entitled to get bonus 
from the II Party /Corporation . Admittedly, the Respondent company is paying bonus to contract 
labourers @ 8.33%. 


AWARD 
As per discussion above, the claim petition filed by the Petitioner Union is liable to be dismissed. 
The reference is answered accordingly.

As per letter dated 12/12/2014 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification No. L- 
12011/233/2001 (IR(B-1)) dt. 12/12/2014. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the Management of State Bank of India, Raipur in terminating the services of Shri 
Beni Ram Sahu w.e.f. 12.08.2000 is justified? If not, to what relief the Workman is entitled for?” 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


Case of the Workman is mainly that, he was initially appointed as temporary part-time General Attendant 
with the Bank w.e.f. 20.12.1993 and worked continuously without any break till 12.08.2000. Prior to 1993, he had 
worked as Badli watchman and waterman with the Bank for intermittent period. He was appointed to the post of 
General Attendant on the basis of interview in which he has been found suitable. His services were terminated by 


7468 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 13, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 22, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Management Bank w.e.f. 12.08.2000. He had worked for more than 240 days in every year and it thus qualified to be 
permanent employee by the Bank on regular basis. By not granting him permanent status after engaging him as 
temporary attendant from 1993 to 2000 Bank has adopted unfair labour practice. It is further his case that, he was 
working as against vacant post and also that, after his disengagement his post was filled by one Shri Ramchandran. 
According to the Workman, this action of Management Bank is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. He has requested that 
holding is disengagement against law, he be held entitled to be reinstated with back wages and benefits. 


Case of the Management Bank is mainly that, the Workman was engaged on temporary basis as part-time 
General Attendant vide order dated 20.12.1993. His engagement was contractual on temporary basis. His services were 
terminated vide letter dated 12.08.2000 after compliance of section 25F of the Act, he was paid Rs. 7084/- as 
compensation and Rs. 810/- for 12 days service in August. He was also paid an amount of Rs. 1024 towards one month 
salary in lieu of notice period. The Management has thus requested that, there is no illegality in their action. 


In evidence, the Workman has filed and proved his interview letter, appointment letter, salary slips. He has 
also filed his affidavit as his examination in chief. He has been cross-examined by Management. He has also examined 
his witness Nakul who is also been cross-examined by Management. Management has filed affidavit of his witness as 
his examination-in-chief. He has been cross-examined by Workman. Management has proved termination letter dated 
12.08.2020, interview letter and appointment letters of different persons with respect to different Branches for the post 
of part-time Temporary General Assistance. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for Workman Mr. Neeraj Kewat. None appeared for Management. 
I have gone through the record as well. 


The reference itself is the issue for determination. 


On perusal of record, in the light of arguments it comes out that, the engagement of the Workman by Bank for 
the period between 1993 to 2000 is not disputed by Bank. According to the Bank they have paid one month salary in 
lieu of notice and compensation in form of 15 days salary for every year he has worked. Hence their action in 
disengaging him is fully legal and justified in law. 


According to workman side, by engaging the Workman as temporary part-time General Assistance Attendant 
for as many as 7 years, the Bank has adopted unfair labour practice. Unfair Labour practice is defined under Section 
2(r)(a) read with Schedule 5(10) of the Act, according to which engaging a person as temporary employee for a long 
time amounts to unfair labour practice on the part of employee. Hence, by engaging the Workman as temporary and 
part time worker for about 8 years the Bank is held to have adopted unfair labour practice in the case in hand. 


Unfair labour practice is prohibited under the Act and is a punishable offence. Their civil consequences are not 
mention in the Act, but it does not deny the Courts and Tribunals in adopting the civil consequence of unfair labour 
practice adopted by employees. 


Much time has been lapsed in the case in hand and Workman would have attained the age of superannuation 
also. Hence, a lump sum compensation will meet the end of justice in case in hand. Keeping all the facts in view, 
a lump sum compensation of Rs. 2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lakhs) to be paid by the Bank to the Workman within 
30 days from the date of publication of Award. Failing which interest @6%, in lieu of all his claims will meet the 
ends of justice in case in hand to which the Workman is held entitled. 


The reference stands answered accordingly.

HAA श्री वीपचन्द बाल्मिकी; HATH वैनिक वेतन Heft TRA संवेशवाहक; को 1.8.1993 स्रे 1.11.2017 तक 
नियोजित में रखने पश्चात्‌ उसकी सेवाएं1.11.2017 से समाप्त किये जाने की कार्यवाही नययोचित है? यदि नहीं तो, 
सम्बंधित आवेबक किस अनुतोष के हकदार हैं ?? 


Case of the workman is mainly that, he worked with the Bank from 01.08.1993 to 30.11.2017 continuously 
as a Peon/Messenger, his services were dispensed with by the Bank without any notice or compensation which is 
unjust, illegal and arbitrary. 

The case of management is that the applicant never worked continuously at any point of time and did not 


complete 240 days in any year, he was disengaged by Bank and just to avoid complications was paid notice pay and 
compensation as provided under Section 25-77 of The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 [in short ‘the Act’]. 


7470 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 13, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 22, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Both the sides have filed their respective affidavits as their Examination-in-chief, they have been cross- 
examined by opposite party, they have filed and proved documents also, to be referred to as and when required. 


I have heard argument of the Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Rajneesh Sharma and Mr. Vijay Tripathi, 
Learned Counsel for Management. Management has preferred written submission also. I have gone through the 
written submission and record as well. 


From perusal of the record, it is established that workman was retrenched on 01.11.2017, whereas the 
notice pay and compensation was given to him by the Bank on 30.11.2017, the issue thus arises for determination is, 
whether by payment of notice pay and compensation after one month from the date of retrenchment, as the 
management Bank acted in violation of Section 25-F of the Act. For the sake of convenience, Section 25-F is 
reproduced as follows:- 


“25F. Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen.—No workman employed in any industry who 
has been in continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be retrenched by that 
employer until— 


(a) the workman has been given one month’s notice in writing indicating the reasons for 
retrenchment and the period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of such 
notice, wages for the period of the notice; 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be 
equivalent to fifteen days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or any part 
thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government or such authority as 
may be specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette.” 


A bare perusal of provision makes it clear that the notice pay and compensation is required to be paid at 
the time of retrenchment i.e., on the date of retrenchment, since in case in hand, the payment has been made after one 
month of retrenchment, it is in violation of Section 25-F of the Act. 


The reference and judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Pramod Jha & Ors. v/s State of 
Bihar, (2003) 4 SCC 619, has been made by Learned Counsel for workman, paragraphs 10 to 15 of the said judgment 
are being reproduced as follows:- 


“10. We have given our anxious consideration to submission and counter-submission made 
before us in the light of the pleadings and undisputed documents available on record. We are of the 
opinion that the appeals are devoid of any merit and liable to be dismissed. The underlying object of 
Section 25F is two-fold. Firstly, a retrenched employee must have one month time available at his disposal 
to search for alternate employment, and so, either he should be given one month notice of the proposed 
termination or he should be paid wages for the notice period. Secondly, the workman must be paid 
retrenchment compensation at the time of retrenchment, or before, so that once having been retrenched 
there should be no need for him to go to his employer demanding retrenchment compensation and the 
compensation so paid is not only a reward earned for his previous services rendered to the employer but is 
also a sustenance to the worker for the period which may be spent in searching for another employment. 
Section 25F nowhere speaks of the retrenchment compensation being paid or tendered to the worker along 
with one month s notice; on the contrary clause (b) expressly provides for the payment of compensation 
being made at the time of retrenchment and by implication it would be permissible to pay the same before 
retrenchment. Payment of tender of compensation after the time when the retrenchment has taken effect 
would vitiate the retrenchment and non-compliance with the mandatory provision which has a beneficial 
purpose and a public policy behind would result in nullifying the retrenchment. 


11. Compliance with clauses (a) and (b) of Section 25F strictly as per the requirement of the 
provision is mandatory. However, compliance with clause (c) is directory, as held in Gurmail Singh and 
Ors. vs. State of Punjab and Ors- (1991) 1 SCC 189 and a substantial compliance would be enough. 


12. Gammon India Limited vs. Niranjan Dass (1984) 1 SCC 509, relied on by Shri Mishra, the 
learned senior counsel for the appellants, has no application to the facts of the present case. There the 
notice under Section 25F (a) stated the reason for retrenchment as "due to the reduction of the volume of 
work of company as a result of the recession". However, the real reason was closure of company s Delhi 
office and there was not even a whisper in the notice of this real reason and the same was sought to be 
disclosed by leading evidence before the Industrial Tribunal which was not countenanced by this Court. 


13. In Gurmmail Singh & case (supra) a three-Judge Bench of this Court examined the question 
of compliance of Section 25F(b). It was contended on behalf of the workers that the State had not. 
furnished the details of the amounts of compensation determined in the case of each employee and that 
the State had not taken steps to deliver the amount in respect of each employee at his doorsteps by the 


[भाग त--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : दिसम्बर 13, 2025/अग्रहायण 22, 1947 7471 


relevant date. It was urged that the tender of compensation under Section 25F, in order to be valid, should 
be of the precise amount and should be made simultaneously with termination of the service. It was found 
that the bank drafts in respect of individual employees were dispatched in time so as to reach 
Divisional/Sub-Divisional Offices of the employer well in advance of the date of expiry of the notice period 
and the date on which the retrenchment was to be effective. The amounts were not actually paid or 
tendered to the workers directly but a method for disbursement of compensation was evolved in the 
interest of workers convenience. Instead of the workers, spread out all over the State, being asked to come 
to the Head Office to collect the amount of compensation and the difficulty of the employer in making 
available the compensation at the doorstep of each employee, an arrangement was made whereby the 
workers could go to the nearest Divisional/Sub-Divisional Office and collect the amount of compensation 
due to them. None of the workers ascertained whether the amounts sent by the Head Office to the 
Divisional/Sub-Divisional Offices were the correct amounts. No instance was pointed out to show that the 
bank drafts were not for the correct amounts. The High Court felt satisfied that the individual 
compensation drafts were sent to the various subordinate offices ready for disbursement to the concerned 
workers on or before the relevant date. It was held that there was sufficient compliance with the provisions 
of clause (b) of Section 25F. This Court agreed with the view of the High Court. 


14. In The Management of Delhi Transport Undertaking vs. The Industrial Tribunal, Delhi and 
Anr. (1965) 1 SCR 998 pari materia provision as to payment of compensation equivalent to one month 
wages to workmen contained in proviso to sub-section (2) of Section 33 of ID Act came up for the 
consideration of this Court. It was held that the proviso did not mean that the wages for one month have 
to be actually paid; the employer is expected to tender the amount before the dismissal but cannot force 
the employee to receive the payment before dismissal becomes effective. The making of the tender of the 
amount, before the order of dismissal becomes effective, would be sufficient compliance. 


15. In Sain Steel Products (supra), which is a two-Judge Bench decision of this Court, the worker 
was informed "to collect what is due to him without spelling out whether or not it included the amount as 
contemplated under Section 25F. It was in such peculiar facts and circumstances of the case that this 
Court refused to accept the offer in the terms in which it was made and quoted hereinabove as amounting 
to making an offer in terms of Section 25F of the Act. Both the Labour Court and the High Court had 
recorded a finding of fact that Section 25F (b) was not complied with. Sain Steel Products Case (supra) is 
clearly distinguishable and has no application to the facts of the present case.” 


In another reported decision, in the case of Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, Rewa v/s Jaiprakash Mishra, 
decided by Hon’ble High Court of 11.72, 2000 (Supreme) MP 880, the same principle has been followed. The 
relevant portions of the said judgment are being reproduced as follows:- 


“In my opinion, it is clear from reading of written statement (P-2) filed by Krishi Upaj Mandi 
Samiti that workman has rendered the services from September, 1990 till December 1991. This fact has 
not been disputed, rather asserted by Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, there is no plea taken that there was any 
interruption in the services in the above period for 15 months, thus petitioner has rendered the services at 
least for 15 months even as per the case set up by Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, thus, Labour Court has 
rightly come to the conclusion that termination is illegal and void for want of compliance of section 25F 
of ID Act. 


Section 25F of the ID Act was considered by the apex Court in M/s National Iron and Steel Co. 
Ltd. and others 7. The State of West Bengal and another [AIR 1967 SC 1206] and it was held by the Apex 


Court that if workman is retrenched without giving one month's notice, his wages for period of notice 


must be paid before he is asked to go. The apex Court has emphasized on the payment of compensation at 
the time of retrenchment. 


The apex Court in Workmen of Subong Tea Estate, represented by the Indian Tea Employees 
Union ० Outgoing Management of Subong Tea Estate and another [AIR 1967 SC 420], has laid down 
that non-compliance of section 25 or section 230 renders the retrenchment invalid. 


The Apex Court in Mohan Lal v. The Management of Mis Bharat Electronics Ltd. [AIR 1981 SC 
1253] has followed its earlier decision in State of Bombay v. The Hospital Mazdoor Sabha [AIR 1960 SC 
610] and has held in para 9 thus: 


9. Reverting to the facts of this case, termination of service of the appellant does not fall within 
any of the excepted, or to be precise, excluded categories. Undoubtedly, therefore, the termination would 
constitute retrenchment and by a catena of decisions it is well settled that where prerequisite for valid 
retrenchment as laid down in section 25F has not been complied with, retrenchment bringing about 
termination of service it ab initio void. In The State of Bombay v. The Hospital Mazdoor Sabha, [(1960) 2 
SCR 866 at p. 872 AIR 1966 SC 610 at p. 613], this Court held that failure to comply with the requirement 
of section 25F which prescribes a condition precedent for a valid retrenchment renders the order of 


7472 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 13, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 22, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


retrenchment invalid and inoperative. In other words, it does not bring about a cessation of service of the 
workman and the workman continues to be in service. This was not even seriously controverted before 


us." In Gammon India Ltd. v. Niranjan Dass [AIR 1984 SC 5001, it has been emphasized by the apex 


Court that when the prerequisite for a valid retrenchment as laid down in section 25F was not complied 


with, the retrenchment bringing about termination of service of employee would be ab initio void. 


In H.D. Singh 7०. Reserve Bank of India and others [AIR 1986 SC 132], law to the same effect has 
been laid down in Ratan Singh 7. Union of India and another ((1997) 11 SCC 396], it has been laid down 
by the apex Court that section 25F is applicable to termination of even a daily-rated workman who had 
continuously served for the requisite statutory minimum period in a year, and termination of service of 
such a workman without compliance of section 25-F was held to be illegal. 


In Management of MCD 7. Premchand Gupta and another [AIR 2000 SC 454], it has been held 
by the apex Court that if retrenchment compensation has not been paid, termination is null and void. 


In Rajkumar 7०. Union of India and others [(1975) 3 SCC 458] considering the similar provision, 


the apex Court has held that pay and allowances should be paid on the day the order of termination is 
served. Delay in payment of saine was held to be fatal. 


In Smt. Kusum Gupta Kusum Bansal v. Haryana State Small Industries and Export Corporation, 
Chandigarh [(1986) 3. SCC 506), the apex Court has laid down considering the similar provision that 
payment of salary in lieu of notice is mandatory. Employer is not entitled to withhold the payment on the 
ground of non-production of ''no dues certificate" by the employee. Termination without such payment 
was held to be invalid.” 


Hence, in light of the aforesaid proposition of law, the retrenchment of the applicant workman in case in 
hand, is held in violation of Section 25-F of the Act and is held against law. 


Now the question arises as to what relief the workman is entitled to when retrenchment has been found 
against law and in violation of the Act? 


The Learned Counsel for workman has referred to judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of 
Tapash Kumar Pal v/s BSNL & Ors, (2014) 15 SCC 313, wherein it has been held that the order of retrenchment can 
be substituted by awarding compensation only on certain justifiable grounds and has submitted that keeping in view 
the tenure of the workman, he deserves to be reinstated with backwages and benefits. 


Learned Counsel for management Bank has opposed this argument and has submitted that the workman was 
not appointed against a sanctioned vacancy, following retrenchment process. He was a daily wager engaged on as and 
when required basis who was paid for that. Hence, he does not deserve to be reinstated or regularized. Learned 
Counsel has referred to following judgments:- 


i. State of Karnataka v/s Umadevi, (2006) 4 SCC 1 

il. Himanshu Kumar Vidyarthi & Ors. v/s State of Bihar, AIR 1997 SC 3657 
iil. B.S.N.L. v/s Bhuramal, AIR 2014 SC 1188 
iv. State of Haryana & Ors. v/s Piara Singh & Ors, (1994) 4 SCC 118 


Though, the management has denied the tenure engagement of the workman but it is established that he was 
paid Rs. 5,372/- as notice pay which is his one month salary and Rs. 55,786/- as compensation. 


As per Section 25-F of the Act, the workman is entitled to compensation, wages of 15 days for one year of 
service he has spent, on this basis when he was admittedly paid compensation of Rs. 55,786/- @ 15 days for every 
year of service, it implies that he had spent more than 20 years, which corroborates the case of the workman that he 
had worked with the Bank, if not from 01.08.1993 to 01.01.2017 then atleast more than 20 years. 


Had he not been retrenched, the workman would have earned about Rs. 5 Lac/- approximately as a salary 
and bonus of a temporary part time employee within the period starting from date of his retrenchment in 2017 till 
date. He would have also been eligible to be considered for appointment as temporary full time worker and permanent 
worker keeping in view his tenure during this period and thereafter post retiral benefits. Keeping these facts in view, a 
lump sum amount of Rs. 10 Lac/- to be paid by Bank within 30 days from the date of publication award, failing which 
interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of award till payment, in lieu of all his claims will meet the ends of justice. 


In the light of the above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows:-

AWARD 


Holding the action of management of State Bank of India in retrenchment of Narayan Prasad Balmiki 
unjust and illegal, he is held entitled to a lump sum amount of Rs. 10 Lac/- to be paid by Bank within 30 days from 
the date of publication award, failing which interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of award till payment, in lieu of all

As per letter dated 07/09/2017 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification 
No. L-12012/86/2016-(IR(B-D) dt. 07/09/2017. The dispute under reference relates to: 

“Whether in the light of Desai Award recommendations contained under Chapter-16 Item No.14 Para No. 
16.9 cited by the Management of State Bank, Raisen MP, the 97 Pay Revision Bi-partite settlement dated 
27.04.2010 isb applicable in the case of Shri Vijay Kumar Lohat, Safai Karamchari, SBI Branch Slamatpur? If 
yes, what benefits/relief the workman is entitled to and from which date?” 

Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


7474 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 13, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 22, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


Case of the workman is mainly that, he was first appointed as a Sweeper on 01.10.1985 in the Slamatpur 
Branch of the Bank having area of 1936.27 Sq. ft. on monthly wages of Rs. 20 per month. His wages were extended 
up to Rs. 190 per month. He used to work more than one hour daily in the Branch for cleaning. Bank had formed a 
policy with respect to creation of posts of part-time sweepers and payment to them with respect to the total area which 
they cleaned. It was provided that, for a total area of 1200 sq. ft. and above but less than 2000 sq. ft. the sweeper was 
required to work six hours to thirteen hours per week and was entitled to 1/3 of scale wages as part-time worker. The 
local head office at Bhopal sent a communication to all the Branches on 18.02.1997. The Branches were asked to 
review after six months and simultaneously, norms for creation of post of General Attendant (sweepers-cum-Farrash), 
where considered necessary, shall also be framed in consultation with the Union. Another communication by the 
Local Head Office at Bhopal to the Deputy General Manager of Zonal Office was sent on 25.02.1997 in this reference 
requesting them to give their priority to the matter and ensure that their recommendations for sanction of post of 
sweepers accordingly reaches to the Local Head Office positively before 10.03.1997, so that further action can be 
taken. 


It is further the case of the Workman that, the applicant workman was appointed on permanent basis as a 
sweeper in the Branch from 12.05.1999 vide letter of the Bank dated 13.02.2001 and hence, was entitled to 1/3 of the 
salary as permanent part-time sweeper, according to the Memorandum of the Agreement, as referred to above, on 
07.02.1997. According to the Workman, the Management did not grant him 1/3 salary which he was entitled to from 
08.05.1999 and issued another appointment letter dated 10.05.2016 appointing him as permanent part-time 
Messenger-cum-Farrash in the Bank on 1/3 of the scale. The Workman has thus prayed that, he is entitled to 1/3 of 
the pay of scale in the light of settlement dated 07.02.1997 from the date of his permanent appointment as part-time 
sweeper which is 08.05.1999 and other consequential benefits. 


The case of Management is mainly that, the Workman was engaged as a daily wager on temporary basis in 
the Slamatpur Branch and used to work as a sweeper accordingly, on as and when required basis. He was appointed as 
a permanent part-time sweeper vide order dated 10.5.2016 on the terms and conditions mentioned in his appointment 
letter which he accepted. He was entitled to 1/3 of the scale, as his wages. Before this date, no appointment was made 
after following any recruitment procedure nor was he engaged against any vacancy, also he did not work 
continuously. The appropriate Government has made this reference regarding entitlement of the Workman to receive 
benefits of 9" Pay Revision by Bi-partite Settlement dated 24.10.2010. The Workman has claimed benefits before this 
period from the date of his initial engagement which is beyond the scope of the reference and is barred by 
unexplained delay and latches on his part. The said settlement is applicable only with respect to the permanent 
workers mentioned in the Para 16.9 of Chapter 16 of the Desai Award. 


According to the Bank, the Settlement dated 07.02.1997 and Circulars dated 18.02.1997 and 25.02.1997 are 
applicable only for permanent part-time employees, and not on persons engaged on temporary basis. Hence, 
according to the Management, workman is not entitled to the relief claimed by him. Also, it has been pleaded that his 
appointment was made by Branch Manager who is not a competent authority to issue an appointment letter. 
Management has thus prayed that reference be answered against the Workman. 


In evidence, the workman has filed his affidavit as his examination in chief. He has been cross-examined by 
Management. He has filed and proved the Memorandum of 07.02.1997, Circulars dated 18.02.1997 and 25.02.1997 
which are Ex. W-1 to W-3. The workman has also filed and proved his appointment as permanent part time sweeper 
in compliance of letter of Zonal Office No. RI/SC/3014 dated 19.06.1999. Also, he has filed and proved his 
appointment letter dated 10.05.2016 and photocopy statement of his account, transfer order. 


Management has filed affidavit of its witness as his examination in chief. He has been cross-examined by 
Workman side. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for the Workman Mr. Arun Patel and Mr. Vickram Johri Learned 
Counsel for the Bank. Both the sides have filed written submissions also. I have gone through the written submissions 
as well. 


The first argument raised from the side of Management is that, this Tribunal is not required to travel beyond 
the reference. The reference has been produced earlier. The Bi-partite Settlement dated 27.04.2010, Chapter 16, Item 
No. 14 (Para 16.9) states that it shall apply only to the permanent employees. According to the Management, the 
Workman was first appointed as a permanent part-time sweeper on 10.05.2016 before this date, he was a daily wager 
employee. 


Case of the Workman is that he was appointed as the permanent part-time sweeper, w.e.f. date of his 
reemployment dated 12.05.1999 vide appointment letter issued by the Branch Manager on 13.02.2001. As the letter 
reads, his appointment is in the light of instructions received from Zonal Office letter No. RI/SC/314 dated 
19.06.1999. Photocopy of this letter is also on record. It states that, that with reference to the letter No. BIO/RI/SC 
156 dated 08.05.1999, the workman was directed by the Zonal Office, to be given permanent appointment effective 
from date of his re employment and direction was issued to issue appointment letter accordingly. It is established 
from this document which is (Ex. W-8 Appointment Letter) that Letter of Assistant General Manager issuing

instructions that the Workman was appointed as a permanent part-time sweeper in the Bank w.e.f. 12.05.1999. His 
statement is on oath also corroborates his case. 


On the other hand, the Management witness states and it is the case of the Management that the Branch 
Manager, who issued the appointment letter appointing the workman from 12.05.1999 did not have authority to do so. 
This argument cannot be accepted because this letter itself shows that, this appointment letter was issued in 
compliance of the instructions of the Zonal Officer vide its letter dated mentioned in the appointment letter itself. The 
instructions letter also corroborates this fact. Hence the argument from the side of the Management that the workman 
was appointed by the Branch Manager who did not have authority to appoint him fails, and it is held that in fact the 
Branch Manager issued only the appointment letter and the instructions to the appointment as well the decision to 
appoint the Workman as permanent part-time sweeper was in fact done by the Zonal Officer of the Bank, hence this 
appointment of the workman w.e.f. 12.05.1999 is not illegal, rather it is perfectly legal. Arguments from the side of 
the Management that, the said settlement dated 27.04.2010 will not apply in the case of the Workman fails because 
the Workman was a permanent part-time sweeper on the date on which the settlement came into force. He is held 
entitled to benefit of Item No. 14 (Para 16.9) Chapter 16 of the settlement. 


As regards, the other arguments from the side of Management that, the Court should not travel beyond the 
terms of the reference. This argument also cannot be accepted. Normally Courts and Tribunals do not travel beyond 
the scope of reference, but they are within their powers to mould the relief and grant reliefs if it is required to meet the 
ends of justice.Section 10 (4) of the Act is being reproduced as follows- 


10(4) Where in an order referring an industrial dispute to a Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal 
under this section or in a subsequent order, the appropriate Government has specified the points of dispute for 
adjudication, the Labour Court or the Tribunal or the National Tribunal, as the case may be, shall confine its 
adjudication to those points and matters incidental thereto. 


Case of the workman is mainly that, in spite of being appointed as a permanent part-time sweeper in the 
Bank he has been not paid 1/3 of pay scale which he was entitled to meet under the Settlement dated 07.02.1997 and 
Communications dated 17.02.1997 and 25.02.1997. It is further his case that the total area of the Bank is 1936.27 sq. 
ft., as per the Settlement dated 07.02.1997 a cleaner is required to work i.e. of 13 hours per week and is entitled to 
receive 1/3 of the pay scale admissible to a permanent full time sweeper from the date of his appointment 1.6. 
12.05.1999.The area of Bank has not been disputed. It has been held proved that the workman was lawfully appointed 
as permanent part time employee as cleaner for the first time 12.05.1999 and the Management Bank is held under 
obligation to pay the Workman one third of scale pay admissible to permanent cleaner from the date his this 
appointment was made effective in his appointment letter dated 12.05.1999. 


No other point was pressed. 
In the light of above findings reference is answered as follows. 
AWARD 


Workman is held entitled to benefit of Bi-partite Settlement dated 27.04.2010 Chapter 16 (Item No. 14) 
Para 16.9. He is also held entitled to benefits of Settlement dated 07.02.1997 and is held entitled to receive 1/3 of 
pay scale admissible to permanent full time sweepers from the date his appointment as permanent part-time

As per letter dated 15/10/2019 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference has 
been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per Notification 
No.J-1(2-5)/2019-IR dt. 15/10/2019. The dispute under reference relates to:- 


“क्या प्रबंधन क्षेत्रीय प्रबंधक; THY बैंक; क्षेत्रीय कार्यात्रय. SMT (oT) / शाखा प्रबंधक; THI बैंक कृषि नगर 
अधारतान, ATA (मध्य प्रवेश के प्रबंधन व्वारा श्री अरुण प्रताप सिंह आत्मज श्री Tera सिह; HATS कैशियर को 
विनांक16.17.2018 & अनिवार्य सेवानिवृत्त किये जाने की कार्यवाही न्यायोचित हैं? यवि नहीं तो; संबंधित आवेबक किस 
HAAS के हकवार हैं?” 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and filed 
their respective statement of claim in defense. 


In his statement of claim, the workman has alleged that the management issued charge-sheet against him on 
18.04.2018 with respect to charges of alleged misconduct viz; disobedience of order and mismanagement of 
cash/shortage of cash, as well misbehaviour with customers. The management conducted a departmental inquiry, which 
was a mere formality. The inquiry was conducted illegally without following principles of natural justice and without 
giving the workman opportunity to cross examine management witnesses, examined during the inquiry, in the light of 
documents filed by the management. It is also alleged that the Inquiry Officer acted with partiality while conducting 
inquiry and acted like a prosecutor, he himself examined the witnesses, the statements of witnesses were recorded in 
absence of workman and he was asked to cross examine such witnesses on their pre-recorded statement. The Inquiry 
Officer permitted leading questions by the Presenting Officer, while examining the management witnesses, documents 


1478 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 13, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 22, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


and materials used against the workman in evidence were not supplied to him. Inquiry Officer relied on CCTV footage, 
which was not provided to the workman inspite of his demand. It is has been further alleged that on 10.07.2018, after 
management had examined its witnesses, the Inquiry Officer permitted the management to produce documents, which 
were admitted on record by the Inquiry Officer inspite of objection. The workman was not given opportunity to further 
cross examine the management witnesses in the light of documents filed later and also the workman was not given 
sufficient time to produce evidence in rebuttal. The charges were held wrongly proved and the punishment is also 
disproportionate. 


The case of management on this issue is that, there is no procedural illegality or material irregularity in 
conducting the inquiry, the workman was issued a charge-sheet of misconduct on 18.04.2018. Before that, a show cause 
notice was issued against him with respect to the allegations and he had submitted his reply dated 18.03.2017 
suppressing the material facts. It was after that the charge-sheet leveling charges of misconduct were issued against the 
workman on 18.04.2018. The workman was given full opportunity to defend himself during the inquiry. He pleaded not 
guilty. The charges were rightly held proved and punishment is not disproportionate. 


Following preliminary issue was framed on the basis of pleadings- 
Whether the departmental enquiry conducted against the workman is legal and proper? 


On the basis of evidence on record, this preliminary issue was decided vide order dated 04.10.2024, the 
departmental enquiry was held just legal and proper. 


Following Additional Issues were framed, thereafter: - 

1) Whether the findings of the enquiry officer with respect to charges can be held perverse? 
2) Whether the punishment awarded is disproportionate to the charges proved? 

Parties were given opportunity to lead evidence on additional issues. They did not lead any evidence. 


I have heard Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Neeraj Kewat and Mr. Sushil Dubey for management Bank. 
I have gone through the record as well. 


Additional Issue No.1, 


The Charge against the workman is that he committed misconduct by way of keeping with him Rs. 500/- out 
of Rs. 55,000/-, which were given to him by the account holder Mohd. Rafiq on 22.09.2007 to be deposited in his 
account, on protest the workman indulged in argument with the account holder, he was seen concealing Rs. 500/- 
currency note and unnecessary argued with the account holder as seen in the CCTV footage. Another charge was on 
24.10.2007, the cash could not be compared till 09:00 pm because it was Rs. 2,000/- more than what it showed in the 
records. It was due to wrong entry made by the workman in the voucher in which he mentioned Rs. 14,000/- in place of 
Rs. 16,000/-. The third charge was that the workman used to work slowly than normal speed and used to misbehave 
with the staff and account holders. Another charge was that he kept Rs. 5,000/- with himself on 10.10.2017, which he 
had received to deposit in bank and deposited it when this default was noticed. Thus according to the management, he 
thus committed misconduct in clause 5(e), 5(g), 50) and 5(q) of memorandum of statement dated 10.04.2002. 


It is settled proposition of law that the nature of evidence required to prove the charge is not it is required to 
prove in a criminal trial, there is on record statements of the witnesses affected, who are members of staff and account 
holders who have corroborated the charges. Reproduction of their statements is not required, the workman side has 
cross-examined these witnesses but there is nothing to discredit them in their cross-examination. Hence, keeping in 
view the nature of evidence collected during the enquiry which is supported by documents also, the finding of enquiry 
officer that the charges are proved is held not perverse. 


Additional Issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. 
Issue No. 2, 


The nature of the charges proved is such that they are acts of moral turpitude; they attract the punishment of 
dismissal from service also. The workman has been ex-serviceman, management has considered the point of 
punishment in light of these facts and awarded him compulsory retirement. 


The settled proposition of law is that until and unless the punishment awarded is so disproportionate to the 
charge proved that it shocks the conscious of the Court, it need not be interfered with. 


In light of nature of charges proved, it cannot be said that the punishment is shockingly harsh. Hence, holding 
the punishment awarded, not disproportionate to the charges proved. 


Issue No. 2 stands answered accordingly. 


In light of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows.-

Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 


defense. 


In the RC/01/2020 case of the petitioner Workman is that, he was appointed as a Driver in the Bank in 
Sector-10 Bhilai Branch since 05.04.2014 and has been continuously working as Driver since then. He has been 
driving Vehicle No. CG/04/KS/4448 Scorpio on requisition of the Bank and has been used by the Bank in its work. 


In the RC/02/2020 case of the petitioner Workman is that, he was appointed as a Driver in the Bank in 
Sector-10 Bhilai Branch since 19.08.2015 and has been continuously working as Driver since then. He has been 
driving Vehicle No. CG/04/KS/4460 Scorpio on requisition of the Bank and has been used by the Bank in its work. 


7482 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA DECEMBER 13, 2025/AGRAHAYANA 22, 1947 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


In the RC/03/2020 case of the petitioner Workman is that, he was appointed as a Driver in the Bank in 
Sector-10 Bhilai Branch since 09.11.2015 and has been continuously working as Driver since then. He has been 
driving Vehicle No. CG/04/KS/4426 Scorpio on requisition of the Bank and has been used by the Bank in its work. 


In the RC/04/2020 case of the petitioner Workman is that, he was appointed as a Driver in the Bank in 
Sector-10 Bhilai Branch since 09.06.2016 and has been continuously working as Driver since then. He has been 
driving Vehicle No. CG/04/HA/9266 Sumo (Cash Van) on requisition of the Bank and has been used by the Bank in 
its work. 


In the RC/05/2020 case of the petitioner Workman is that, he was appointed as a Driver in the Bank in 
Sector-10 Bhilai Branch since 01.10.2014 and has been continuously working as Driver since then. He has been 
driving Vehicle No. CG/07/AT/7654 Swift on requisition of the Bank and has been used by the Bank in its work. 


The Workmen used to maintain the logbook in this respect. Bank used to bear the petrol and other expenses 
with respect to the vehicle. The vehicle was registered in the name of Bank; their wages were paid by the Bank and 
also their bonuses. The Bank merged with Bank of Baroda with all its assets and liabilities and even after the 
petitioners has been working as Drivers of these vehicles. They were disengaged by the Bank on 31.08.2019 without 
any notice or compensation which is unjust, illegal and arbitrary and is in violation of the Section 25F and 25G of the 
Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 (in short the “Act’). They raised a dispute with Labour Commissioner (Central) at Raipur 
in this respect, which could not be conciliated within 45 days. Hence, they have filed these petitions under Section 2- 
A (2&3) of the Act, seeking relief of setting-aside their termination and thier reinstatement with all back wages and 
benefits. 


In all these cases, the case of Management taken by them in their written statement of defense is mainly 
that, there was no sanction vacancy of any Driver in the Dena Bank and in Bank of Baroda after merger of Dena Bank 
with Bank of Baroda vide notification dated 02.01.2019. The petitioners were not appointed by Bank under any 
recruitment process. According to Bank, the vehicles are provided to certain Officers and petrol expenses as well 
Driver expenses incurred by the Officers are reimbursed by the Bank. It is further the case of the Management Bank 
that, the Petitioners were engaged by the concerned officers who used these Bank vehicles for Bank purposes and 
paid these petitioners their wages which was later on to them reimbursed by Bank. Hence, according to the Bank there 
was no employee and employer relationship between petitioner and the Bank. Hence, there is no question of 
disengagement of the petitioners by the Management Bank. In their rejoinders filed by the petitioner in response to 
the written submissions by Bank, they have mainly reiterated their case. 


In all these cases, the petitioners filed their affidavits as their examination-in-chief, wherein they mainly 
reiterated their allegations in the petition. They were cross-examined by the Management, they admitted in their 
cross-examination that no formal appointment letter was issued to them, no recruitment process was organized for 
their appointment and their attendance was never marked in the attendance register of Bank employees. 


In all these cases, the Bank has also filed affidavit of its witness as his examination-in-chief. Petitioners 
have not cross-examined the witness in these cases. 


No documentary evidence have been filed by the petitioners in any of these cases. The Bank has filed a copy 
of circulars collectively marked as M-1. 


I have heard argument of Mr. N.L. Shrivastava Learned Counsel for the Workman and Mr. Anoop Nair 
Learned Counsel for the Management Bank, assisted by Learned Counsel Mr. Neeraj Kewat in all these cases and I 
have gone through the record. 


Since, the facts as well the nature of dispute and evidence in all these cases is identical these cases are being 
disposed by the Common Judgment and Award. 


On perusal of record, in the light of rival arguments following issues arises for determination — 


1. Whether there exists employer-employee relationship between the petitioners and the Bank at any 
point of time? 


2. Subject to finding on Issue No.1, whether the petitioners are entitled to relief sought? 
Issue No. 1 - 


Pleadings of the parties on these issues have been elaborated earlier. Except affidavits of the petitioners, 
there is no document on record to corroborate their cases. There are some photocopy documents filed by them but not 
proved. These documents show that the petitioners were the personal drivers of the Officers. Their admission in their 
cross-examination that they did not undergo any recruitment process and that they were not issued any formal 
appointment letter also militates against their case. 


On the other hand, there is uncontroverted affidavit of the Management witness who has not been cross- 
examined by the petitioner’s side, which corroborates the case of the Management. Thus, circular filed show that 


[भाग 1--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : दिसम्बर 13, 2025/अग्रहायण 22, 1947 7483 
certain Officers are provided Bank vehicles for which they were reimbursed the expenses on drivers engaged by them 
and petrol etc. 


In the judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the Case of Bank of Baroda V.s. Ghemarbhai Harjibhai 
Rabari 2005 SCC (L&S) 963, three judge bench of the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that, the onus of prove that the 
claimant was in employment of Management lies on the person to show claims. 


Hence, in the light of above discussion and findings, it is held that the petitioners have failed in proving 
employer and employee relationship between them and the Bank. 


Issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. 
Issue No. 2 — 
In the light of aforesaid findings, the Issue No. 2 is answered accordingly. 


The judgments of Ghaziabad Development Authority V.s. Vikram Chaudhary MPWN (1995) SC 179, Tula 
ram V.s. State of M.P. 2013 (1) MPWN 27, Ramdayal Jat V.s. Laxmi Prasad 2010 (III) MPJR (SC) 1, Smita 
Shrivastava V.s. State of M.P. 2024 (2) JLJ 635 SC, will not apply in the cases in hand. In the light of findings there 
is no employee — employer relationship between the parties. 


No other point was pressed. 


In the light of above discussion and findings, the aforesaid petitions are sans merit and are liable to be 
dismissed. 


ORDER 
Petitions dismissed. 
Copy of order to be placed on the files all the cases. 
No order as to cost.
